docs.title: KendoDojoManagement
docs.text: Self-hosted web application for managing the members, sessions, and attendance of a kendo dojo. Single-dojo per instance, deployed with rootless Podman.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Members — full profile management with grade history, coach/first-aider flags, and under-18 safeguarding fields
  • Sessions — recurring templates and ad-hoc sessions with per-type colour coding, iCal feed, and a calendar/list toggle view
  • Attendance — self check-in, one shareable check-in link per session, admin overrides, and visitor records
  • Grades — enforced kendo grade progression (Mukyū → 8-dan) with full audit trail
  • Federations — per-member federation memberships with membership numbers and renewal tracking. The catalogue starts empty; add the federations your dojo uses in Admin Settings. The FIK affiliate list is the authoritative source for official names, abbreviations and websites.
  • Reports — attendance and member-grade reports with CSV export
  • Auth — passkey (WebAuthn) primary, recovery codes, admin-issued recovery tokens, and break-glass CLI token
  • Security — rate limiting, account lockout, security headers, CORS, and structured security event logging

docs.title: Container runtime
docs.text:
Podman is the supported runtime. It is what the project is developed and tested against, and what both deployment paths target: rootless, daemonless, systemd-native.

Docker is best-effort and unverified. The Compose files use no Podman-specific syntax and the Makefile auto-detects docker compose, so it is expected to work — but nothing here is tested under Docker and no parity is promised. Bug reports are welcome; behaviour differences are not treated as release blockers.

Every command in these docs is written in its podman / podman-compose form. With the podman-docker shim installed, docker and docker compose are aliases for these, so both spellings work; a clean Podman install has no docker binary at all, which is why the Podman form is the one written out.

Compose files keep their docker-compose.*.yml names — that is the filename Compose implementations look for by convention, and -f names them explicitly at every call site regardless of runtime.

docs.title: Deployment paths
docs.text:
Two supported ways to run this in production — pick one:

Path Files Use when Compose docker-compose.yml + .env + kendo-app.env You want a single host up quickly. Traefik terminates TLS on 80/443 with a Let's Encrypt certificate over the HTTP challenge. See Quick self-host. Quadlet deploy/quadlet You want the hardened deployment: rootless systemd units, Traefik with automatic TLS, network segmentation, Podman secrets, automated backups. ./setup.sh --quadlet lays it all down; full runbook in Hardened deployment.

docs.title: Architecture review — August 2026
docs.text:
Deepening opportunities found by walking the hot spots of the preceding ~50 commits. Vocabulary is deliberate: module (interface + implementation), interface (everything a caller must know, not just the signature), depth (behaviour per unit of interface), seam (where an interface lives), adapter (a thing satisfying an interface at a seam), leverage (what callers gain), locality (what maintainers gain).

Two rules of thumb applied throughout: the deletion test — if deleting a module concentrates complexity it earns its keep, if it merely moves it the module was a pass-through — and one adapter is a hypothetical seam, two is a real one.

Candidate 01 (the duplicated Federation Membership card) shipped as #361. The four below are open, in the order I would take them.

docs.title: 02 — "What a Member may see of a Session" has no home
docs.text:
Strength: strong.

Files: backend/app/sessions/router.py (~280–350), app/sessions/ical.py, app/sessions/models.py.

Problem. Three read paths each re-derive the same rule in their own handler body:

  • GET /sessions composes _strip_coach_notes(_strip_cancelled(...));
  • GET /sessions/{id} writes result["coach_notes"] = None inline and does not filter cancelled sessions;
  • ical.py carries a third, prose-documented allow-list.

_normalize_instance must additionally be remembered at five call sites. This is an authorisation rule scattered across handlers: it is reachable only through an ASGI request, so every test of it costs an authenticated client, and a fourth read endpoint is correct only if its author copies carefully.

Proposed shape. app/sessions/projection.py, owning one question — what does a caller with this Role see?

visible_session(record, *, role)
visible_sessions(records, *, role)

Behind that interface: normalisation to SessionInstanceRead, cancellation filtering, and admin-only field redaction. Handlers keep what is genuinely HTTP. This is the shape app/sessions/templates.py established for the Session Template lifecycle in #352, applied to reads instead of writes.

Payoff. The next admin-only field on a Session is redacted once. Redaction becomes a table test with no request, no DB, no fixtures — alongside test_checkin_window.py, which already has that shape.

docs.title: 03 — The repository seam speaks dict[str, Any]
docs.text:
Strength: worth exploring. Right direction, wrong as a big bang.

Scale: 240 occurrences across 26 modules under backend/app/; backend/tests/fake_repositories.py is 673 lines.

Problem. Every repository Protocol returns an untyped dict, so the interface is not the signature — it is every key name, every "this is an ISO string, not a date" convention, and every default, none of which a type checker can hold. The cost is visible: callers write date.fromisoformat(template["start_date"]), routers re-apply _normalize_* to fill missing optionals, and the fake repositories re-implement the dict shaping the real ones do, because the shape is written down nowhere else.

History confirms it hurts. #345 "settle the date type at the repository seam"; #345 "delete the date guards the member stubs were propping up"; #348 "one member fake for eleven partial stubs".

Proposed shape. Repositories return the Pydantic Read models models.py already defines. The seam does not move; only its currency changes. SessionInstanceRead becomes the return type, _normalize_instance disappears, and the fake constructs the same model as the real repository. app/member_federations/ already has a typed MemberFederationRecord — the precedent exists.

Sequencing. One repository per PR under the existing red-green slicing, starting with sessions. Judge after the first before spreading.

docs.title: 04 — The load / save / error ladder, repeated
docs.text:
Strength: worth exploring.

Files: AdminSettingsPage.tsx (47 useState, 1405 lines), MemberDetailPage.tsx (36), SessionDetailPage.tsx (27), SettingsPage.tsx (20).

Problem. Every card re-declares the same ladder — data, loading, loadError, saveStatus, saveError — plus a useEffect(fetch).then(set).catch(setError) and a try/catch save handler. Each is a shallow module: the interface (the state names) is as large as the implementation (two setters and a fetch), and nothing is shared, so changing how API failures surface is a thirty-site edit.

Proposed shape. Two hooks in frontend/src/lib/, built on the request/isApiError module api/client.ts already centralises (#343):

useResource(fetcher, deps)  -> { data, error, reload }
useAction(fn)               -> { run, status, error }

Deliberately stops short of TanStack Query, which brings caching and invalidation nobody has asked for.

Payoff. Cards shed ~10 lines of state plumbing each and become nearly pure render functions, which the existing __tests__/ suite is good at.

docs.title: 05 — The current User is fetched once per page
docs.text:
Strength: speculative. Listed for completeness; do not start here.

Files: App.tsx plus six pages calling getMe(); 45 isAdmin references; contexts/DojoSettingsProvider.tsx and contexts/ThemeProvider.tsx as the established pattern.

Problem. The Role of the current User is global knowledge being re-derived locally, then threaded down as a prop.

Why it stays speculative. The duplicate fetches are cheap, the threading is harmless, and isAdmin as an explicit prop makes components easier to render in tests than a context would. Revisit if a third Role appears and the boolean stops being enough.

docs.title: Incidental findings
docs.text:

  • UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md gained Federation Membership with #361. No CONTEXT.md or docs/adr/ exists in this repo, so no candidate here contradicts a recorded decision — there are none to contradict.

docs.title: Calibrating AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS
docs.text: Issue #268. Supersedes the unmeasured 50ms default introduced with the constant-time floor in #255.

docs.title: What the setting does
docs.text:
The passkey "begin" endpoints answer for any email, registered or not, so that a caller cannot tell the two apart from the response. The real path (known email, valid invite) does strictly more work than the decoy path — an extra SELECT, a pending_challenge UPDATE, a commit — and #255 measured that asymmetry at a ~2ms median delta: enough to enumerate registered emails from latency alone.

ConstantTimeAuthMiddleware closes it by holding every request to these paths for a fixed minimum wall-clock time:

  • POST /auth/login/passkey/begin
  • POST /auth/invites/redeem/begin

Two heavier endpoints have floors of their own, calibrated in Login complete and recovery redeem: LOGIN_COMPLETE_MIN_DURATION_MS for POST /auth/login/passkey/complete and RECOVERY_REDEEM_MIN_DURATION_MS for POST /auth/recovery/redeem.

The masking only works while the real path finishes under the floor. Once a real request overruns it there is nothing left to pad, and the delta is observable again. So the floor has to sit above the real path's p99 — which is what this document measures, because 50ms was picked as a round number and never checked against PostgreSQL.

docs.title: How to reproduce the measurement
docs.text:
The harness is backend/tests/test_auth_begin_calibration.py. It is skipped unless AUTH_BEGIN_BENCH=1, so it costs the normal suite nothing.

docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm \
  -e PYTEST_TARGET=tests/test_auth_begin_calibration.py \
  -e AUTH_BEGIN_BENCH=1 \
  -e AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS=1 \
  -e RATE_LIMIT_PER_IP=1000000/minute \
  -e PYTEST_ADDOPTS=-s \
  test > /tmp/bench.log 2>&1

The floor is dropped to 1ms so the measurement captures the endpoint's own work rather than the pad, and the per-IP rate limit is lifted because every sample arrives from one address. Those two overrides belong only to this command. Together they disable the timing-side-channel defence and the brute-force rate limit; never copy them into a deployed environment file. The harness itself cannot run anywhere dangerous — conftest.py refuses any DATABASE_URL that is not a PostgreSQL database with "test" in its name — but the env vars would apply anywhere. It seeds real accounts, members and invites; drives 1000 measured requests per scenario over real HTTP against the uvicorn that run_tests.sh starts; and then asserts the side effects only the real path produces, so a seeding mistake cannot quietly report decoy-path timings as good news.

Two views come out of one run. The harness prints client-observed latency. The numbers below are the server-side elapsed that ConstantTimeAuthMiddleware logs — with the floor at 1ms its "floor exceeded" warning fires on every request and carries the elapsed time. That is the quantity the floor is actually compared against, so it is the one the default has to clear. Extract it with:

grep -a "floor exceeded" /tmp/bench.log

docs.title: Measured results
docs.text: Environment: docker-compose.test.yml (PostgreSQL 16, default fsync=on), podman on WSL2, developer workstation, 2026-08-10. n=1000 per row after 50 discarded warmup requests. All figures in milliseconds, server-side.

docs.title: Sequential — one request at a time
docs.text:
endpoint p50 p90 p95 p99 max login/passkey/begin 7.4 9.0 9.6 11.0 14.2 register/passkey/begin 12.1 14.3 15.1 16.7 27.9 invites/redeem/begin 12.4 14.4 15.1 16.8 23.8

Real-path p99 is 16.8ms; the worst single request out of 3000 was 27.9ms.

docs.title: Under concurrency
docs.text: Swept on register/passkey/begin, then the heaviest repeatable path (removed in

docs.title: 472; a new run sweeps login/passkey/begin). "over 50ms" is
docs.text:
the share of requests that would have breached the old default.

in-flight requests p50 p90 p99 max over 50ms 1 12.1 14.3 16.7 27.9 0% 2 15.1 18.0 22.1 30.0 0% 4 33.1 38.6 45.7 53.2 0.3% 8 67.1 89.3 167.0 183.0 98.5% 12 108.0 153.5 281.1 339.2 100% 20 206.6 356.7 534.7 553.6 100%

Latency is dominated by queueing, not by the database: past ~4 simultaneous requests the single uvicorn worker's event loop is the bottleneck and every figure scales with concurrency.

docs.title: Re-measured for #432 — one email, on the Member
docs.text:
#432 changed every query on these paths: users.email is gone, and an Account is found by joining its Member on members.email. Registration and invite redemption now create the Account from a Member id (invite redemption creates that Member first when there is none). Same command, same environment class, 2026-10-03:

endpoint p50 p90 p95 p99 max login/passkey/begin 5.0 5.7 5.9 6.5 32.9 register/passkey/begin 5.3 6.0 6.3 6.8 11.0 invites/redeem/begin 7.8 9.0 9.4 10.5 20.7

Server-side, sequential, n=1000 per row after 50 warmups. The join costs nothing measurable: every p99 is below the August figures, which says more about the workstation on the day than about the change. The worst single request, 32.9ms, is a third of the 100ms floor, so the default stands. The concurrency sweep kept its shape: queueing past ~4 requests in flight, as above.

Parity between known and unknown emails is a separate check, and it is still the one that gates: test_passkey_timing.py and test_timing_convergence.py assert that the real and decoy paths converge, and both pass against the new queries.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The default is raised from 50ms to 100ms.

  • At the concurrency a single-dojo instance actually sees, the real path's p99 is 16.8ms and its observed worst case 27.9ms. 50ms did clear both — the old default was not wrong, just unevidenced.
  • It did not clear them by much. These numbers come from a developer workstation; the real path's cost is dominated by the commit, and a production volume on modest VPS storage can be several times slower than an overlay filesystem on a laptop. A 2× slower commit puts the observed maximum at ~56ms, past the old floor. 100ms absorbs that; 50ms does not.
  • The pad itself is cheap. The unit-of-work commits and releases its connection inside the measured region, so a padded request holds an idle asyncio task and no database connection. At the 20/min per-IP limit, doubling the hold time changes in-flight occupancy by a fraction of a request per source — the DoS analysis in #266 is unaffected.
  • 100ms is still well below the threshold at which a user notices latency on a deliberate action like starting a login.

No floor survives a saturated server. At 8 simultaneous begin requests the p99 is already 167ms, and holding that would need a floor an order of magnitude above anything sane. Raising the floor is not the remedy for saturation:

  • The condition is detectable. ConstantTimeAuthMiddleware logs a warning naming the elapsed and configured times on every overrun. Alert on it.
  • The remedy is capacity or rate limiting — a second worker, or a tighter RATE_LIMIT_PER_IP — not a larger AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS. Reaching 4+ simultaneous begin requests requires many distinct source addresses, given the 20/min per-IP limit, which is itself the signal worth acting on.

docs.title: Login complete and recovery redeem (#594)
docs.text:
#594 put two more endpoints behind the middleware, each with its own floor:

  • login/passkey/complete. #587 made a known and an unknown email do the same work before a credential matches. That left no margin: its timing test failed on the pre-fix code by only 0.03ms. A floor gives a margin that does not depend on the machine.
  • recovery/redeem. #588 padded the bcrypt work, but a known email still did database work an unknown one skipped, about 12ms: the lockout lookup, reading its codes and tokens, and writing a failed attempt.

The harness is test_measure_redeem_and_login_complete_latency, in the same file and behind the same flag:

podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm \
  -e PYTEST_TARGET=tests/test_auth_begin_calibration.py \
  -e "PYTEST_ARGS=-k redeem_and_login_complete" \
  -e AUTH_BEGIN_BENCH=1 \
  -e AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS=1 \
  -e LOGIN_COMPLETE_MIN_DURATION_MS=1 \
  -e RECOVERY_REDEEM_MIN_DURATION_MS=1 \
  -e RATE_LIMIT_PER_IP=1000000/minute \
  -e PYTEST_ADDOPTS=-s \
  test-backend > /tmp/bench.log 2>&1

The warning about the overrides above applies here too.

  • Login complete is measured on a successful login, its heaviest path: signature check, sign count, a new Auth Session, a commit. The harness signs real assertions with a P-256 key.
  • Redeem is measured on its slowest path: a known email with a full code set and an admin token, sending a wrong code. All nine hashes are compared at cost 12, and a failed attempt is written. Each Account is used once, so none reaches the lockout.

Same environment class as above, 2026-11-12. Milliseconds, after warmups.

endpoint n p50 p90 p95 p99 max login/passkey/complete, success, seq 1000 19.1 22.0 22.9 26.1 105.2 login/passkey/complete, success, c=4 1000 49.0 58.5 61.6 70.6 203.2 login/passkey/complete, success, c=8 1000 96.9 113.9 119.4 163.6 250.2 recovery/redeem, known, seq 200 1902.9 1949.0 1970.7 2018.8 2148.5 recovery/redeem, unknown, seq 200 1906.0 2193.5 2237.0 2337.0 2521.2 recovery/redeem, known, c=2 200 2333.8 2448.3 2494.9 2568.8 2619.1 recovery/redeem, known, c=4 200 2346.5 2452.9 2635.9 3016.9 3061.1

The redeem rows are server-side, from the middleware's warnings. The login complete rows are client-observed, because the endpoint had no floor yet to log one. Over loopback, that adds well under a millisecond. Redeem takes seconds per request, so its rows have 200 samples, and each p99 rests on two.

LOGIN_COMPLETE_MIN_DURATION_MS defaults to 250ms. Its worst single request one at a time, 105ms, already passes the begin endpoints' 100ms floor, so complete needs a floor of its own. 250ms is 2.4 times that worst case. It also clears every request at 4 in flight, and the p99 at 8.

RECOVERY_REDEEM_MIN_DURATION_MS defaults to 5000ms. That is 2.1 times the worst sequential p99, the unknown email's 2337ms, and 1.6 times the worst request at 4 in flight. bcrypt is CPU-bound, so a slower VPS core scales the whole figure, not only the commit. Recovery is rare and deliberate, so a 5-second answer costs a user little.

The Conclusions above hold for both floors. A "Constant-time floor exceeded" warning names the endpoint and its setting, and it is a capacity signal, not a reason to keep raising the floor.

docs.title: The convergence assertion's own false-failure rate
docs.text: Separately from the floor, backend/tests/timing_support.py asserts that the real and decoy paths converge in latency. Its tolerance is calibrated against the noise in the run being judged, but floored at the 1ms budget inherited from

docs.title: 255 — so on a quiet run, where 3 × control falls under that floor, the
docs.text:
calibration is switched off by its own lower bound and the run is judged against a flat 1ms. Every observed false failure lived in that regime (#364): same-path controls of 0.08–0.20ms against cross-path deltas of 1.12–1.34ms, on three unrelated branches including main.

Raising the floor is not available as a remedy — it is the #255 budget, and it would eat the margin MAX_TOLERANCE_S deliberately leaves under the ~2.02ms leak that issue measured. Instead a tripped assertion is re-measured from scratch and fails only if it reproduces (assert_latency_converges_sampled). A false failure is a per-run sampling accident; a real asymmetry is present on every run.

Measured by Monte Carlo, two branches drawn from an identical distribution at the #298 noise level (±3ms spread, n=31, 100,000 trials):

rounds required false-failure rate 1 5.503% 2 (shipped) 0.317%

Detection is unaffected for every leak shape the suite has a fixture for; the per-shape figures and the one shape that does pay for it are tabulated in the timing_support.py module docstring. Cost is one extra sampling round on the failing path only.

docs.title: Why a confirmed failure is worth reading
docs.text:
#360 asked for the delta to be measured directly, isolated and under load, before any bound was touched — a load-dependent real asymmetry and a sampling accident look alike in a single run. Sampling the redeem-begin pair over 15 rounds per condition, varying only the number of tasks contending for the event loop:

contending tasks signed median delta valid slower control 0 +0.001 ms 8/15 0.173 ms 1 −0.019 ms 7/15 0.149 ms 2 +0.005 ms 8/15 0.136 ms 4 +1.514 ms 15/15 1.139 ms

Unloaded, the delta is nil and its sign is a coin flip — the fingerprint of a sampling accident, and the regime every observed false failure came from. Under real contention the sign stops flipping, and the middleware logs Constant-time floor exceeded ... 169.3ms elapsed vs 20ms floor alongside it. That is not the harness misreading noise: the real path's work has overrun AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS, the floor has stopped masking it, and while the load lasts the asymmetry is as visible to an attacker as to the test.

docs.title: 360 poses the choice as inherent to the endpoint, fix at source versus
docs.text:
load-induced, make the calibration load-robust. The measurement says neither. The observed false failures had quiet controls (0.08–0.20 ms), and the quiet rows above show no delta to be robust to — under 0.02 ms, sign random. They are accidents in the tail of that distribution. The loaded row is a different event, and a true positive: the floor really has stopped masking, so damping it with a quiet phase or a load term would suppress the one reading worth having. What remains is to tell accident from asymmetry by whether it recurs.

Confirmation therefore suppresses the accident without suppressing the unmasking — the accident gets a fresh coin and mostly does not recur, the unmasking holds for as long as the machine is busy. So 0.317% is the floor of the achievable rate rather than a promise, and a failure that survives both rounds should be read as check whether the floor was exceeded — which is what the assertion message now says.

docs.title: CI reports these assertions; it does not gate on them
docs.text:
Since the confirmation round shipped, this assertion has failed 2 of 6 runs on GitHub's hosted runners — against the 0.317% predicted above. Both failures reproduced across both rounds, so whatever drives them persists rather than resampling away, and the independence the 0.317% assumes does not hold there.

Neither documented mechanism explains it. The most recent failure had:

  • same-path control 0.026 ms — an exceptionally quiet run, not a contended one
  • cross-path delta 1.317 ms
  • no Constant-time floor exceeded warning anywhere in the run, so every request finished inside the floor and both paths should have been padded to the same total

Two hypotheses were tested and ruled out:

Hypothesis Test Result Response length differs between paths Compared bodies directly Byte-identical, 1045 both — #354's equalisation holds Residual is the post-response UoW teardown, outside the padded region Raised the floor 20 ms → 200 ms under identical load +3.529 ms → +0.072 ms. A residual outside the padded region could not be absorbed by a larger floor, so it is inside it

So the local contention case is understood (the real path approaches the floor, the mask stops working, a larger floor absorbs it) and the CI case is not.

The same unexplained shape also shows up locally, so it is not specific to GitHub's runners. On 2026-11-09, test_invite_redeem_begin_valid_vs_invalid_median_latency_converges failed in a local full-suite run (Podman, docker-compose.test.yml, the test service) on the #593 branch. That branch does not touch the invite or floor-middleware code. The failure:

  • same-path control 0.098 ms
  • cross-path delta 1.225 ms, n=31, reproduced on both rounds
  • no Constant-time floor exceeded warning

The same test passed in the full run before it, on the same branch, and when tests/test_invites.py was rerun alone straight afterwards. During #589 it also failed once and passed on two reruns.

docs.title: Explained: the pad's own wake-up (#596)
docs.text:
#596 found the cause. The delta was never in the endpoint's work or in teardown. It was in how late the pad's asyncio.sleep(remaining) woke up, and that depended on remaining.

On Linux, asyncio's EpollSelector rounds a timeout up to whole milliseconds as math.ceil(t * 1e3) * 1e-3. For some k, the float k * 1e-3 lands just above k/1000 (18 * 1e-3 == 0.018000000000000002), and CPython's epoll.poll rounds it up again. A timeout of k ms then waits k+1 ms. Up to 200ms the affected values are 9, 13, 18, 26, 36, 52, 59, 67, 71, 72, 87, 103, 104, 118, 119, 134, 142, 143, 144, 174 and 175.

Under the invite test's 20ms floor, the decoy path had 17.x ms left to pad. That rounds up to 18 and waited 19ms. The real path had 16.x ms, which rounds up to 17 and waited 17ms. Which path lands in a bad bucket depends on how fast the machine runs the handler. That is why the failure came and went with load and runner, why its sign flipped, and why it reproduced on both rounds with a quiet control and no floor-exceeded warning.

The earlier test that "ruled out" a residual outside the padded region was taken under contention: the +3.529ms row is the loaded case. It never measured the quiet case. In this test the residual couldn't be teardown anyway: DbSessionUnitOfWork, which DB-backed tests use, does nothing on exit.

Measured with probes on the middleware, the service and each ASGI send, Python 3.13.18, median sleep overshoot past the pad's deadline:

run valid invalid median delta result isolated 0.67ms 1.79ms −0.98ms pass, just under tolerance full backend suite ×2 0.51–0.52ms 1.72–1.78ms −1.20 / −1.21ms fail on both rounds fixed, full suite ×2 0.002ms 0.002ms +0.024 / −0.015ms pass fixed, one shared CPU ×3 0.003–0.004ms 0.003–0.004ms +0.017 / +0.101 / −0.200ms pass

The pad now sleeps to 5ms short of its deadline and yields the rest (_sleep_until in app/core/middleware.py). The coarse sleep woke at most 2.36ms late on one shared CPU, so 5ms leaves room. The cost is at most 5ms of yielding per padded request. tests/test_constant_time_pad.py pins the property: two handlers whose remaining time rounds up to 18 and to 17 must end together.

This is a production fix, not only a test fix. With the 100ms floor, bucket 87 is hit when a path's work takes 13–14ms. That would have shown about a 1ms real-versus-decoy difference over HTTP.

The CI step below stays advisory until runs on GitHub's runners show the delta has gone there too.

Given that, .github/workflows/backend-tests.yml marks the three wall-clock assertions timing_sensitive and runs them in a continue-on-error step. The numbers stay visible for anyone investigating, while unrelated PRs stop being painted red — a check that cries wolf trains people to re-run without reading, which is how a real regression gets waved through. The strict assertion is kept where a human is already reading output: a local run, and the full suite on release-candidate tags (tests.yml), which does not exclude them.

A green push is therefore not evidence these converged. If the advisory step fails on a run whose control is not unusually quiet, investigate rather than dismiss.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Measured on a developer workstation, not on UAT or production hardware. The 100ms figure carries deliberate headroom for that reason, but it is not a substitute for the real thing. The cheapest confirmation is the one #268 suggests: check UAT/production logs for "Constant-time floor exceeded". If it never fires under real use, the floor is comfortable. If it fires regularly on an unsaturated instance, the real path there is slower than measured here and this document should be re-run and revised.
  • The measurement uses one uvicorn worker, matching the deployed container. Adding workers would move the concurrency knee but not the sequential figures.
  • These are server-side times. A client also pays network latency, which does not help an attacker — it is added to both the real and the decoy path.

docs.title: Hardened deployment
docs.text:
What an operator graduates to from the Quick self-host: a hardened, self-hosted deployment on rootless Podman + Quadlet, fronted by Traefik for automatic HTTPS. Primary target: AlmaLinux 10 (Podman 5.x). A Debian/Ubuntu stub is at the end.

Architecture at a glance. The app image serves both the built SPA and the /api from one FastAPI container on port 8000. Three containers run per host:

           :80/:443 (host)
               │
         ┌─────▼─────┐        kendo-edge (external)
         │  traefik  │◄───────────────┐
         └───────────┘                │
                                 ┌─────▼─────┐   kendo-backend (isolated)
                                 │    app    │◄──────────────┐
                                 └───────────┘               │
                                                       ┌──────▼─────┐
                                                       │  postgres  │
                                                       └────────────┘
  • kendo-edge — Traefik ↔ app. Traefik is the only container publishing host ports.
  • kendo-backend — app ↔ db, no host ports. The db lives only here, so nothing outside this network can reach it.
  • Both networks set Options=isolate=true, which blocks traffic to containers on other Podman networks while leaving internet egress intact (Traefik still reaches Let's Encrypt).
  • The app straddles both networks; the db is reachable only from the app.

All artifacts referenced below live in deploy/.

UAT and PROD are separate hosts, one instance each. The Quadlet units, Traefik config, and scripts are identical between them — only the per-host env file values and secrets differ.

docs.title: 1. One-time host preparation (as an admin / sudo user)
1.0 Encrypt the disk
docs.text:
The Postgres data volume, the uploads volume and the local backups all sit on this host's disk and hold every Member's personal data, including under-18 and safeguarding data. Use full-disk encryption, so a stolen disk, a copied VM snapshot or a decommissioned drive gives none of it away:

  • Your own hardware or hypervisor: choose LUKS ("Encrypt my data" in the AlmaLinux installer) when installing the OS; adding it later means a reinstall. The host then waits for the passphrase at every boot. For unattended reboots, bind it to the TPM with Clevis.
  • Cloud VM: turn on the provider's encrypted volumes for the boot disk and any data disks.

This protects the disk while it is powered off, not a running host. Backups leave the disk, so they carry their own encryption: see The backup key and Off-site copies.

docs.title: 1.1 Install Podman
docs.text:
sudo dnf install -y podman   # AlmaLinux 10 ships Podman 5.x
podman --version             # confirm >= 4.4 (Quadlet); 5.x expected

docs.title: 1.2 Allow rootless binding of ports 80/443
docs.text:
Rootless containers can't bind ports <1024 by default. Write the one-line sysctl drop-in:

echo 'net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=80' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-kendo-rootless-ports.conf
sudo sysctl --system

Trade-off: any unprivileged process may now bind ports ≥80 — fine on a single-purpose appliance. Hardened alternative (keeps the <1024 restriction): leave the sysctl out, set Traefik to publish 8080:80/8443:443, and add a firewalld redirect: 

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-forward-port=port=443:proto=tcp:toport=8443
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

docs.title: 1.3 Open the firewall
docs.text:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

docs.title: 1.4 Create the dedicated rootless user kendo
docs.text:
A no-login system account owns and runs every container. It is never in sudo/wheel and is never logged into directly.

sudo useradd --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin kendo
# Verify subuid/subgid ranges exist (auto on AlmaLinux 10); add if missing:
grep -q '^kendo:' /etc/subuid || echo "kendo:200000:65536" | sudo tee -a /etc/subuid
grep -q '^kendo:' /etc/subgid || echo "kendo:200000:65536" | sudo tee -a /etc/subgid

# Linger: start the kendo user manager at boot, keep services running with
# nobody logged in.
sudo loginctl enable-linger kendo

docs.title: 1.5 Get an admin shell as kendo
docs.text:
Always use machinectl — it sets up a proper session bus and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, so systemctl --user works. (su - kendo does not and will leave systemctl --user broken.)

sudo machinectl shell kendo@ /bin/bash
# You are now kendo, with a working user systemd session.

Name the shell: kendo's login shell is nologin, so it can never be logged into directly, and without one machinectl shell ends at once with This account is currently not available.

Everything from here (sections 2–6) runs as kendo via machinectl shell.

docs.title: 2-4. Lay it all down (as kendo)
docs.text:
# Extract the deployment bundle from the release image — no clone, no build.
# The bundle ships inside the image it configures, so the units below and the
# app they start are one artefact (ADR-0004).
mkdir -p ~/src && cd ~/src
podman run --rm ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:0.1 init | tar -x

./setup.sh --quadlet

setup.sh --quadlet asks for the domain, the TLS option and the ACME challenge, then does every mechanical step that used to be three sections of transcription here:

  • the six secrets — kendo_postgres_password, kendo_migration_database_url, kendo_database_url, kendo_jwt_secret, kendo_setup_token, and the DNS-provider token when DNS-01 is chosen. kendo_migration_database_url is the superuser's login and has to embed the same password as kendo_postgres_password; one script generating both cannot mismatch them. kendo_database_url is the app's own login, kendo_app, which can only read and write rows (ADR-0007): kendo-migrate is the only unit given the superuser, and it creates kendo_app and sets its password from the secret on every start. A re-run keeps every existing secret rather than rotating it.
  • the ~/kendo/ tree — kendo-app.env with your domain in all three passkey-bound settings, traefik/traefik.yml with your ACME email and the challenge you picked, traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml with your Host() rule. Plus ~/backups and the backup/restore scripts in ~/.local/bin.
  • the Quadlet units — copied into ~/.config/containers/systemd/, pinned to the tag the bundle was extracted from, then systemctl --user daemon-reload. Plus kendo-ip-retention.timer and kendo-backup.timer in ~/.config/systemd/user/, enabled — see IP retention below and Backups.

It never escalates: the host prerequisites from section 1 are detected and the exact sudo command printed for you to run from your admin account (kendo has no sudo). Run as kendo, it cannot read the firewall rules either, so it asks you to check those yourself rather than failing.

./setup.sh check --quadlet is the preflight, and is safe to run at any time — after an upgrade, after a domain change, or pasted into a bug report. It checks what the app cannot see from inside its container: placeholders left in ~/kendo/, the Host() rule against WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, the certificate the TLS option needs, the podman secrets, DNS for the domain, whether 80/443 are already taken, and the section 1 prerequisites. Every FAIL names its fix and makes it exit non-zero; a warn (DNS resolving to a router's public address behind NAT, say) is informational. It changes nothing and gates nothing — the app still guards its own configuration at startup.

The setup token is printed once. A podman secret cannot be read back, so the value that claims the first admin account (ADR-0003) is shown at the end of the run and nowhere else. Lost means rotate (below), not recover.

Then check, and start the stack:

./setup.sh check --quadlet                     # green? then:
systemctl --user start kendo-traefik.service   # Requires= pulls in app -> migrate -> db
systemctl --user status kendo-db kendo-migrate kendo-app kendo-traefik --no-pager
podman ps
By hand, without setup.sh 
# Config tree the Quadlet units expect at ~/kendo/
mkdir -p ~/kendo/traefik/dynamic ~/backups ~/.local/bin
cp deploy/traefik/traefik.yml            ~/kendo/traefik/traefik.yml
cp deploy/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml      ~/kendo/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml
cp deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example      ~/kendo/kendo-app.env
cp deploy/bin/kendo-backup.sh            ~/.local/bin/ && chmod +x ~/.local/bin/kendo-backup.sh
cp deploy/bin/kendo-restore.sh           ~/.local/bin/ && chmod +x ~/.local/bin/kendo-restore.sh
Then edit the placeholders: - `~/kendo/kendo-app.env` — set `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID`, `WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN`, `CORS_ORIGINS` to your real domain. Leave `TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true` (required behind Traefik — see §6). - `~/kendo/traefik/traefik.yml` — set the ACME `email`, and swap the challenge if HTTP-01 does not suit (§5). - `~/kendo/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml` — set the `Host(...)` rule to your domain. The secrets. These never touch a plaintext env file. Generate strong values and pipe them in (avoid leaving them in shell history — note the leading space or use `read`): 
# 1. Postgres password
printf '%s' 'REPLACE-with-strong-db-password' | podman secret create kendo_postgres_password -

# 2. JWT secret
python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))" | tr -d '\n' \
  | podman secret create kendo_jwt_secret -

# 3. The superuser's login, for kendo-migrate only (must embed the SAME
#    password as #1)
printf '%s' 'postgresql+asyncpg://kendo:REPLACE-with-strong-db-password@kendo-db:5432/kendo' \
  | podman secret create kendo_migration_database_url -

# 4. The app's own login (ADR-0007), with a DIFFERENT password. kendo-migrate
#    creates the kendo_app user and sets its password from this.
printf '%s' 'postgresql+asyncpg://kendo_app:REPLACE-with-another-strong-password@kendo-db:5432/kendo' \
  | podman secret create kendo_database_url -

# 5. Setup token — gates claiming the first admin account (ADR-0003). Create it
#    BEFORE first boot: the app refuses to start without it, and whoever holds
#    it is who can claim admin.
openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n' \
  | podman secret create kendo_setup_token -
A sixth, `kendo_dns_token`, only when you use DNS-01 — with the drop-in from §5. The units mount each secret as a file under `/run/secrets`, readable only by the app's user, and tell the app where it is with `_FILE` (for example `JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt_secret`). None is passed as an environment variable, so none shows up in `podman inspect` or is inherited by a process the app starts (#462). Then the units: 
mkdir -p ~/.config/containers/systemd
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.network   ~/.config/containers/systemd/
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.volume    ~/.config/containers/systemd/
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.container ~/.config/containers/systemd/

# Quadlet generates systemd units from these files on daemon-reload.
systemctl --user daemon-reload

# Quadlet generates no timers, so the daily IP-retention trigger and the
# nightly backup are plain user units (see IP retention below).
mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user
cp deploy/systemd/kendo-ip-retention.timer ~/.config/systemd/user/
cp deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.service deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.timer ~/.config/systemd/user/
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now kendo-ip-retention.timer kendo-backup.timer

The DB host in DATABASE_URL is kendo-db — the container name, resolved by Podman's DNS on the kendo-backend network.

This is why that network uses Options=isolate=true rather than Internal=true (#281): Podman disables DNS on internal networks, so kendo-db would not resolve and kendo-app could never connect. isolate=true keeps DNS while still blocking cross-network traffic by IP. The trade is that the database keeps an outbound route; on Podman that cannot be removed without also losing name resolution.

To rotate a secret later: podman secret rm <name> then recreate, and systemctl --user restart the affected unit. For kendo_database_url that is kendo-migrate kendo-app: the migration step is what sets the app user's new password, and restarting kendo-app alone does not re-run it.

Because the user has linger enabled and the units declare WantedBy=default.target, the stack now starts automatically on boot. No enable step is needed for .container units generated by Quadlet — the [Install] section handles it after daemon-reload.

Watch the first cert issuance:

podman logs -f kendo-traefik   # look for successful ACME / certificate obtained

Migrations run as their own unit: kendo-migrate.service runs alembic upgrade head and exits, and kendo-app is ordered after it, so the app never serves against a half-migrated schema and a failed migration shows up as a failed kendo-migrate.service rather than as an app crash (#391). systemctl --user status kendo-migrate --no-pager (as kendo) shows whether the last run failed; its log, with the reason, is read from the admin account (see Logs):

sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-migrate.service --no-pager

docs.title: IP retention
docs.text:
recovery_attempts stores the IP address of each recovery-code attempt, and the app clears it to NULL once the row is 30 days old (#434). kendo-app does that on every start; kendo-ip-retention.timer runs kendo-ip-retention.service (python -m app.cli clear-expired-ip-addresses, then exits) daily, so the limit holds on an instance that is never restarted. Persistent=true catches up a run missed while the host was off. ./setup.sh check --quadlet fails while the timer is not installed or not enabled.

systemctl --user list-timers kendo-ip-retention.timer --no-pager
systemctl --user status kendo-ip-retention --no-pager   # did the last run fail? its log: see Logs

The Compose stack has no timer: there the clear runs only when the app starts.

docs.title: 5. TLS options
docs.text:
setup.sh --quadlet asks this question and writes the answer; this section is what it writes, for a deployment configured by hand or changed later.

  • HTTP-01 (default). Needs inbound port 80. Nothing beyond the httpChallenge block already in traefik.yml.
  • TLS-ALPN-01. Inbound 443 only — the answer when an ISP blocks 80. Replace the httpChallenge block with tlsChallenge: {}.
  • DNS-01. No inbound ports at all (e.g. UAT on a local network). Replace the httpChallenge block with a dnsChallenge naming your lego provider, and give Traefik the credentials as a drop-in — the unit itself stays provider-neutral, and a drop-in survives taking a new unit from a release:
printf '%s' 'REPLACE-with-provider-token' | podman secret create kendo_dns_token -
d=~/.config/containers/systemd/kendo-traefik.container.d && mkdir -p "$d"
printf '[Container]\nEnvironment=CF_DNS_API_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/dns_token\nSecret=kendo_dns_token,type=mount,target=dns_token\n' > "$d/10-dns-01.conf"
systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user restart kendo-traefik

CF_DNS_API_TOKEN is Cloudflare's variable (scope the token to Zone:DNS:Edit on one zone); use whichever your provider documents. A provider that needs several variables needs one Environment=/Secret= pair each. - Bring-your-own cert (internal CA / purchased wildcard). For hosts that can't use Let's Encrypt. See deploy/traefik/dynamic/byo-cert.yml.example — it documents the certs/ bind mount (with the required :Z SELinux label) and the router change. setup.sh --quadlet writes both, the mount as a 20-byo-cert.conf drop-in; the cert and key are yours to drop in ~/kendo/traefik/certs/.

docs.title: 6. Why TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true is required behind Traefik
docs.text:
With Traefik in front, every request's peer IP is Traefik's container IP. The app's rate limiting is keyed on client IP — left unadjusted every visitor shares one bucket, so a single busy client exhausts the limit for everyone. Setting TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true makes the app read the real client IP from X-Forwarded-For.

This is the only rate limiting in the deployment: Traefik's dynamic config carries a security-headers middleware and no RateLimit.

This is safe only because of the network design: the app publishes no host ports and is reachable solely through Traefik, which overwrites any client-supplied X-Forwarded-For (do not enable forwardedHeaders.insecure on Traefik's entrypoints). The flag defaults to false so local dev — where the app is directly reachable — stays spoof-proof.

docs.title: 7. A note on CORS
docs.text: The SPA is served same-origin with the API (both under https://<your-domain>), so CORS never fires in normal operation. Keep CORS_ORIGINS pinned to the single canonical origin (never *) — auth is cookie-based, and * + credentials is both invalid and a credential-leak risk. Pinning means any accidental cross-origin path fails closed.

docs.title: 8. Container limits
docs.text:
kendo-app, kendo-migrate, kendo-ip-retention and kendo-traefik assume they may be breached (#458): a read-only root filesystem (/tmp and the volumes are the only writable paths), every capability dropped (Traefik keeps NET_BIND_SERVICE for 80/443), NoNewPrivileges=true, and a cap of 256 pids and 512 MiB memory each. kendo-db is not hardened yet.

The limits are fixed defaults in the units. To change one on a small or busy host, add a drop-in. A later PodmanArgs= flag wins over the unit's own, and the drop-in survives taking a new unit from a release:

d=~/.config/containers/systemd/kendo-app.container.d && mkdir -p "$d"
printf '[Container]\nPodmanArgs=--memory=1g --pids-limit=512\n' > "$d/30-limits.conf"
systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user restart kendo-app

The Compose stack carries the same settings (x-hardening in docker-compose.yml). There, set mem_limit: or pids_limit: on the service itself, which wins over the merged defaults.

docs.title: 9. Logs
docs.text:
The app writes its logs to the container's stdout. Podman's default journald log driver hands them to the kendo user's journal, tagged with the kendo-app unit, so the journal on the device is where they live. Nothing is written to a log file inside the container (the root filesystem is read-only).

# as kendo: this container's output since it started
podman logs kendo-app

# as your admin account (sudo): the unit's history, across restarts
sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-app.service --no-pager

kendo cannot read the journal itself on a default AlmaLinux/RHEL host: as kendo, journalctl prints "No journal files were opened due to insufficient permissions". There is no per-user journal file unless journal storage is persistent, and the system journal is readable only by root and the systemd-journal, adm and wheel groups. So read it from the admin account, by kendo's UID. Do not use --user-unit under sudo: it matches root's UID and shows nothing.

The same command reads any unit's log: swap in kendo-migrate, kendo-backup, kendo-traefik or kendo-ip-retention. Add --since "1 hour ago" (or a time, --since "11:06") to start at a failure. systemctl --user status shows only the last few lines, so it usually cuts off why a unit failed.

docs.title: Security events
docs.text:
Sign-ins, recovery, passkey and invite changes, the setup claim and the other security events are one JSON object per line:

{"timestamp":"2026-10-30T21:31:58.723232+00:00","event_type":"setup_claim","result":"success"}

timestamp (UTC, ISO 8601), event_type and result are always there. user_id, ip_address and detail appear when they apply; every event raised while serving a request carries the client's ip_address.

Sign-in and account events, with result success or failure:

event_type When login_passkey someone signs in with a passkey passkey_registered an Account adds a passkey passkey_deleted an Account removes a passkey recovery_redeem someone redeems a recovery code or admin recovery token admin_token_generated an Admin mints a recovery token for a Member (detail names the target) invite_minted an Admin creates an invite invite_revoked an Admin revokes an invite invite_redeemed someone redeems an invite setup_claim someone claims the first Admin Account with the SETUP_TOKEN sign_out_everywhere an Account signs out of every session

Admin writes and exports are logged too, with the Admin as user_id:

event_type When detail member_created an Admin adds a Member member_id member_updated an Admin edits a Member, including changing their status (deactivation, archiving) member_id, changed_fields member_erased an Admin erases a Member member_id dojo_settings_updated an Admin changes dojo settings, or uploads a logo or login background changed_fields report_exported an Admin downloads a CSV report report, and date_from / date_to for attendance

changed_fields lists field names only. The values, old or new, are never logged. Reading data is not logged.

To see only these lines:

# as your admin account (sudo)
sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-app.service -o cat --grep '"event_type"'
# or pretty-print them, if jq is installed
sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-app.service -o cat --grep '"event_type"' | jq .

docs.title: How long they survive
docs.text:
journald decides, not the app. Check two things as an admin user:

  • Storage is persistent. If /var/log/journal does not exist, the journal lives in /run and every event is gone at reboot. Create it with sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal && sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald, or set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.
  • Size caps. SystemMaxUse and SystemMaxFileSize in /etc/systemd/journald.conf bound the journal's disk use. When the cap is hit the oldest entries go first, so on a small or busy disk events can vanish sooner than you expect. Check with journalctl --disk-usage.

Events carry client IP addresses, which are personal data, so keep them no longer than you need. The app clears IPs from its own recovery-attempt records after 30 days; matching that in the journal is a drop-in:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d
printf '[Journal]\nMaxRetentionSec=30day\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/30-retention.conf
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald

MaxRetentionSec is host-wide: it applies to every service's logs, not just kendo-app.

docs.title: Collecting them off the host
docs.text:
Optional. Any collector that reads the journal works, and the app needs no configuration for it: for example Grafana Alloy into Loki, Graylog, or systemd-journal-remote.

The limit to be honest about: anyone who controls the host can delete events the collector has not pulled yet. Pulling often keeps that window small; it does not close it.

docs.title: Appendix — Debian / Ubuntu stub (not the primary target)
docs.text:
The above is written for AlmaLinux 10. On Debian/Ubuntu the shape is identical; the differences:

  • Podman version. Debian 12 ships Podman 4.3 — too old for Quadlet. Install ≥4.4 from the Kubic/OCI repo or use Ubuntu 24.04 (Podman 4.9). Ubuntu 24.10+/newer is smoother.
  • No SELinux (AppArmor instead) — the :Z volume labels are harmless no-ops; leave them.
  • Low ports / firewall. net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start works the same via /etc/sysctl.d/. Use ufw instead of firewalld for the redirect alternative.
  • User/linger/machinectl — useradd, loginctl enable-linger, and machinectl shell all work identically (systemd-based).

TODO (future): validate and expand this section against a real Debian/Ubuntu host, and consider a GHCR-published image so these hosts skip the build toolchain.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Authentication has no password column. Passkeys are the only login path (#155); accounts carries the WebAuthn challenge fields and nothing else. recovery_codes and admin_recovery_tokens hold bcrypt hashes; invites.token_hash is a deterministic sha256 digest (it is looked up by value — see app/auth/invite_service.py for why that differs).
  • recovery_attempts retention (#434). A successful attempt deletes that Account's earlier rows, leaving only the success. Rows that remain (an Account that keeps failing) are kept as its audit trail — lockout counts only failures from the last 24 hours, and none from before the Account's latest admin or CLI recovery token (#580) — but ip_address is cleared to NULL once a row is 30 days old (IP_RETENTION in app/auth/attempt_repository.py). The clear runs for all Accounts on every app start and, under Quadlet, daily from kendo-ip-retention.timer (#467), so an address outlives 30 days by at most a day. The Compose stack has no timer: there it runs only at app start, and an address can outlive 30 days until the next restart.
  • One WebAuthn ceremony per Account (#435). accounts.pending_challenge / challenge_issued_at hold a single challenge, so a second concurrent registration or login for the same Account overwrites the first, which then fails. A known single-flight limit, accepted at dojo scale.
  • Every Account belongs to exactly one Member (#432, ADR-0006). accounts.member_id is a live link and is enforced: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and a foreign key to members.id with ON DELETE RESTRICT (Members are deactivated or anonymised, never hard-deleted). Most Members have no Account. The email lives once, on the Member — members.email is both the contact address and the sign-in identifier; accounts has no email column.
  • members.claim_attempted_at marks a claim attempt's Member (#446). The first-admin claim creates its Member and Account at begin; this is set on a Member that claim created and cleared when it completes. Completing a claim deletes every other marked Member with its Account, so an attempt abandoned under a mistyped address leaves nothing behind. This is the one hard delete of a Member, and it is safe only because such a Member was never a real one: a Member already on the roster is never marked. Two cases are left for an admin to archive by hand: a claim begun at the instant another completes, and an attempt abandoned before this column existed.
  • Audit columns are not foreign keys. attendance.recorded_by, grade_history.assigned_by and members.anonymised_by record which Account acted. They are deliberately not FK-enforced, so the id outlives the Account it names: erasing a member deletes their Account, and the history that Account recorded must not cascade with it.
  • grade_history.display_name is deliberately denormalised (#435). It is derivable from grade today, but it records what was displayed at the time of the Promotion, which is the point of an audit table.
  • Constraints beyond keys (#431). The database, not just the app, refuses:
  • uq_attendance_session_member — UNIQUE (session_id, member_id) on attendance: a member is checked in at most once per session. NULLs are distinct, so any number of visitor rows (member_id NULL) per session stay legal. This, not the router's existence check, decides a concurrent double check-in (the loser gets 409).
  • ck_attendance_member_xor_visitor — CHECK on attendance: exactly one of member_id / visitor_name is set.
  • uq_member_federations_member_federation — UNIQUE (member_id, federation_id): one membership per member per federation.
  • uq_dojo_settings_single_row — a unique index on the constant (true): dojo_settings holds one row.
  • uq_federations_name — UNIQUE federations.name.
  • uq_session_instances_template_slot — UNIQUE (template_id, original_date) on session_instances (#578): one Session per slot of a series. original_date is the date the template generated the Session for and survives a move, so reconciling a series matches on it rather than on date. Ad-hoc Sessions have neither, so stay unconstrained.
  • ck_members_email_lowercase — CHECK email = lower(email) on members (#592). Sign-in looks a Member up by exact match on the lowercase form LenientEmail produces, so this also makes the UNIQUE on members.email case-insensitive in effect.
  • Index policy (#418). No indexes beyond those that keys and constraints create and the index=True lookup columns on the ORM. Add one when a query is measured slow — at dojo scale a sequential scan is microseconds.
  • federations.source/source_key mark the rows the bundled FIK affiliate list owns (source = 'fik', keyed by ISO code or a body's slug; #613). kendo-migrate syncs them on every run; Admin-added rows have both null.
  • Federation membership is a table, not a column. members has no federation_number: a member can hold numbers with several federations, so it lives in member_federations (dropped from members in #297 — see a5b6c7d8e9f0_drop_federation_number_from_members.py).
  • Sessions are segmented. session_templates/session_instances carry no single session_type_id/start_time/duration_minutes. Each session has one or more segments, each with its own start_time/duration_minutes/ optional public title/position, and each segment links to one or more session types via the *_segment_types join tables (also ordered by position). A session's time envelope (for calendar display) is derived as min(segment start) → max(segment end) — see app/sessions/envelope.py. Segments have no notes of their own: per-segment coach_notes went in #190 and the public per-segment note in #406. Prose about a session belongs in the session-level info (public) or coach_notes (admin-only).
  • session_instances.title is required (no longer derived from session type).
  • session_instances.checkin_window_* override the dojo-wide defaults in dojo_settings when set; null means "use the dojo default".
  • All *_segments/*_segment_types child rows cascade-delete with their parent (ondelete="CASCADE" at the DB level, cascade="all, delete-orphan" at the ORM level) and are fully replaced (delete+recreate) on update — there is no row-level PATCH of an individual segment.

docs.title: The app serves the SPA and the API from one origin, with the API under /api
docs.text: The built SPA is copied into the app image and served by FastAPI itself, and every API router is mounted under an /api prefix, so browser and API share a single origin in development, the quick self-host and the hardened deployment alike. /health (used by container healthchecks) and the /static/* upload mounts stay at the root.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The frontend already called /api/..., but the routers were mounted at the root and Vite's dev proxy rewrote the prefix away. That worked only in development: in both production stacks / and /api/* returned 404, because nothing served the SPA and no route answered the prefixed paths — despite docs/deployment.md describing exactly this arrangement. Single-origin also keeps cookie-based auth and WebAuthn simple: no CORS preflight on the app's own calls, no cross-site cookie rules, one origin for WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN to match.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: Letting the reverse proxy own the split instead — Traefik routing /api to the backend with a StripPrefix middleware and / to a separate SPA container — was rejected. It contradicts the hardened deployment's single kendo-app container, adds a container and a middleware to production for no gain, and leaves the app image unable to serve itself when run without a proxy.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The SPA catch-all mount is conditional on static/index.html existing, so the development image (which runs from source, with Vite serving the frontend) does not need a build step. Vite's /api rewrite is gone: development and production now use identical URLs, which is what makes a proxy in front of the dev stack meaningful at all — see ADR-0002.

docs.title: Traefik runs in the development stack
docs.text: The development Compose stack runs Traefik in front of the app, serving https://dojo.localhost:8443 with a locally-generated certificate, and .env.dev sets COOKIE_SECURE=true and TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true to match the hardened deployment.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A reverse proxy in a dev stack looks like gratuitous machinery. It is there for three behaviours that are otherwise exercised for the first time in production: passkey ceremonies bound to a real WEBAUTHN_RP_ID/WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN over TLS, Secure session cookies, and the X-Forwarded-For path that rate limiting and account lockout depend on. Each of these fails silently or not at all in a plain-HTTP localhost:5173 stack, and each produces a healthy-looking deployment that rejects logins or mis-attributes client IPs.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: dojo.localhost needs no /etc/hosts entry (browsers resolve *.localhost to loopback) and is a secure context, so it beats a .test domain. Ports 8443/8080 are used rather than 443/80 so that running the dev stack does not require the net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start sysctl; the port appears in WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN but not in WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, which stays the bare host. Traefik is configured through the file provider, as in deploy/quadlet — the socket-based label provider was rejected there deliberately and copying it into development would diverge exactly where the point is to match.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The dev certificate is now on the critical path for any authenticated work: with COOKIE_SECURE=true and browsers refusing WebAuthn on a page with a certificate error, an untrusted certificate presents as a healthy stack that cannot hold a session — so make certs reports what it issued and reissues a self-signed pair once mkcert appears, and the README carries the trust-store split a container cannot resolve on the developer's behalf (#379).

The direct :5173 and :8000 ports stay published as an escape hatch when a certificate is missing or HMR misbehaves through the proxy, so the proxy is never the only way in. Vite needs explicit HMR client settings to serve through it, derived from DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN so that the no-proxy runs (the test container, a bare npm run dev) keep dialling their own origin. Host and scheme come from that origin; the client port is pinned only when the origin names one, so a portless origin behind a proxy on 443 leaves Vite to infer the port from the page and keeps its direct-websocket fallback (#380). server.ws is server-wide and Vite's direct-websocket fallback is skipped once a client port is pinned, so exactly one of the two published origins can have HMR: DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN is interpolated with the proxy origin as its default, and emptying it hands HMR to the :5173 escape hatch — which matters when the reason for taking that hatch is HMR misbehaving through the proxy (#382). allowedHosts turned out to be unnecessary: Vite allows localhost and any *.localhost host header before it consults that list. The test stack deliberately does not get Traefik: the e2e suite drives Vite and uvicorn in one container, and an ~11 minute suite should not grow a proxy hop for fidelity it does not test.

docs.title: Claiming the first admin account requires a pre-provisioned setup token
docs.text: The operator provisions a SETUP_TOKEN before first boot — a podman secret under Quadlet, a value in .env for the Compose self-host, each reaching the app as a mounted file — and POST /api/setup/passkey/complete requires it. The app reads it from config like any other secret, compares it in constant time, and refuses to start without it. /api/setup/passkey/begin requires it too (see the amendment under Consequences); GET /api/setup is unchanged, and the existing _has_registered_user() guard still runs first, so a claimed instance stays 404 regardless of what token is presented.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
/api/setup, /api/setup/passkey/begin and /api/setup/passkey/complete are unauthenticated and guarded only by _has_registered_user() — count( PasskeyCredential) > 0 — and complete promotes whoever finishes the ceremony to role="admin". Until someone deliberately finishes, anyone who loads the page takes the dojo (#388).

Counting credentials rather than users is correct and stays: an abandoned ceremony leaves a user row with no credential, and counting those would lock out an operator whose browser died mid-registration. The consequence is that the window never closes on its own.

The hostname is not a secret. Traefik's Let's Encrypt certificate reaches the certificate transparency logs the moment it is issued, so a public deployment is discoverable by an opportunistic scanner within minutes of first boot — plausibly before the operator has opened a browser. The only mitigation today is a paragraph in docs/deployment.md telling the operator to claim the account immediately, which asks them to win a race they were not told they were in until they read it.

That opportunistic scanner is the realistic attacker, not someone targeting this dojo by name. The LAN UAT box and the public PROD box therefore differ in exposure but not in the right policy: the LAN box is simply one the attacker rarely reaches, and a policy that only PROD gets is a policy that is wrong on the day a UAT box gets a public DNS name. One policy covers both.

The deployment already has the shape this needs. deploy/quadlet/kendo-app.container mounts each podman secret as a file readable only by the app's uid, and names the file to the app in <NAME>_FILE:

Secret=kendo_jwt_secret,type=mount,target=jwt_secret,uid=1001,gid=1001,mode=0400
Environment=JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt_secret

The Compose self-host mounts the same files from secrets/, which setup.sh writes from .env. app/config.py resolves every secret through read_secret: <NAME>_FILE when set, the plain <NAME> variable otherwise (the fallback dev and test use). A new secret is a pair of unit lines, a podman secret create and a read_secret call. Nothing in the app has to learn a new way to hold a secret, and nothing has to learn a new way to hand one to the operator.

When this was decided, secrets reached the app as environment variables (type=env). #462 moved them to mounted files, because a variable shows up in podman inspect and /proc/<pid>/environ and is inherited by every child process. The decision is unchanged.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
A pre-provisioned SETUP_TOKEN (chosen). It is config, not state: no table, no migration, no process-scoped value to re-fetch, and no retrieval path to invent. It survives restarts, which matters under Restart=always — a crash-looping unclaimed instance must not invalidate the token the operator is part-way through using. It does not require shell access from the person who claims the account, so an operator can hand a URL and a token to a dojo secretary. Rotation is podman secret rm/create plus a restart.

Its costs are real and accepted. It adds a step before first boot, which the deployment runbook must carry. The plaintext exists wherever the operator generated it — shell history, unless they pipe it (openssl rand -base64 32 | podman secret create kendo_setup_token -). Under Compose there are no podman secrets, so it lives in .env (and the secrets/ file setup.sh writes from it) beside the database password: the same exposure class as what is there, not a new one.

A token generated at boot and printed to the container log. Attractive because podman logs kendo-app is already in the day-2 table, and it needs no provisioning step. Rejected on the Quadlet specifics. Container stdout goes to journald, so the token persists at journald's retention rather than in something ring-buffer-shaped, and log aggregation would carry it off-box; "the token dies with the process" bounds its validity, not where the string is written. Worse, Restart=always means an unclaimed instance that crash-loops issues a fresh token per restart, silently invalidating the one the operator copied a minute ago and failing their correctly-filled form with a 401. The runbook would have to say "re-read the logs after any restart", which is a bad instruction to have to give during first setup.

A token minted through the CLI (app/cli.py, alongside create-recovery-token), retrieved with podman exec kendo-app .... This works with no extra wiring — podman exec sees the same DATABASE_URL_FILE the app reads — and keeps the secret out of the journal. Rejected because it needs persisted token state, a table and a migration, to deliver a secret that config can carry for free, and because it makes shell access a hard requirement for first setup, which forecloses handing a URL to a non-technical dojo secretary.

A pre-seeded admin email in the env file, with setup refusing any other address, carries no new secret and uses a value the operator already sets per host. Rejected as insufficient alone: it authenticates an address, not a person, so a scanner that guesses or learns the dojo's contact address is back inside the window. It narrows the race rather than closing it.

Binding the window to a boot deadline — setup answers only within N minutes of process start — composes with anything here but does not stop this attacker. A CT-log scanner arrives within minutes of first boot, inside any window generous enough not to strand an operator on a slow start, and the option adds a liveness and clock dependency for that partial benefit. Not adopted; revisit only if the token proves insufficient.

Keeping setup open and making it observable would be the honest minimum if the current design were right for this threat model. It is not: the problem is an unbounded window on a publicly discoverable host, not the absence of a signal about it. The observability is not lost — an unclaimed instance still logs one startup line saying so, carrying the claim URL and no secret.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
A missing SETUP_TOKEN fails startup, claimed or not. It joins _REQUIRED_STARTUP_VARS in app/config.py alongside JWT_SECRET and DATABASE_URL, so a misconfigured deployment dies at boot with a named error instead of booting into a claimable instance. Validating it only while the instance is unclaimed was considered and rejected: it needs a database query in lifespan() to decide, and it invites an operator to delete the secret after claiming — which boots fine until the day the database is restored or wiped, and then fails at exactly the wrong moment. One unconditional rule is smaller and fails in the safe direction. .env.example gains the variable, and development needs a value like any other required secret.

Redeploy against an existing database does not reopen anything. Claimed state lives in PasskeyCredential rows; the existing guard runs first, so a restarted or upgraded claimed instance returns 404 as it does today. The token is a second gate in front of that guard, never a replacement for it — and an instance whose token leaks after it is claimed is not thereby claimable.

Amended by #589. Counting passkeys broke that last promise: the only Admin may delete their only passkey while holding recovery codes, which left no PasskeyCredential row and reopened the claim to anyone holding the token. The guard (now _is_claimed()) counts Admin Accounts instead. Admin is granted only when a claim completes (#432), so an abandoned ceremony's Account is a member and still does not count. Nothing removes the last Admin Account: barring the last Admin who may sign in is refused, and erasure needs another signed-in Admin. So the latch needs no migration and no new state.

No migration and no new state. The token is a config value compared with secrets.compare_digest at complete. It travels as an X-Setup-Token header rather than a body field: the request models are shared with the ordinary registration route, and a header keeps the secret out of them and out of anything that logs a request body. GET /setup stays open so the SPA can decide whether to render the setup page.

Amended during implementation (#402). begin is gated too. This ADR originally left it open on the grounds that it closes nothing complete does not already close. That is true of the claim itself, but not of the side effects: begin on an unclaimed instance runs the bootstrap branch of _get_or_create_user, which writes a user row with role="admin" for any email a stranger submits. Leaving it open lets an unauthenticated scanner accumulate admin-roled credential-less rows. Both endpoints now call one shared _require_setup_token() — one place to get the check wrong, not two — after _has_registered_user(), so 404 still wins on a claimed instance.

The same amendment closes the route the original decision missed entirely. POST /api/auth/register/passkey/begin is unauthenticated and reaches the same bootstrap branch, so gating only /setup/* would have left the claim open to anyone who read the OpenAPI schema. The branch is therefore gated where every caller routes through it — register_passkey_begin and register_passkey_complete take allow_bootstrap, which only the setup router passes, and only after the token check. On an unclaimed instance the ordinary registration route now answers with the same decoy it gives an unknown email on a claimed one.

Amended by #472. There is no ordinary registration route any more: Members join by invite only. POST /api/auth/register/passkey/begin is removed, /complete refuses every request with the generic 401, and allow_bootstrap and _is_bootstrap are gone. register_passkey_begin and register_passkey_complete now serve the setup router alone, so the token check in front of them is the only gate the claim needs. The decoy /complete still takes the shared request model, so the header stays.

Lockout is a rotation, not a rebuild. An operator who loses the token recreates the secret and restarts; nothing in the database has to change. The existing break-glass path does not cover a never-claimed instance and is not being stretched to — app/cli.py create-recovery-token resolves a User row by email, and on an unclaimed instance there is none. That gap is acceptable because rotation costs seconds.

The runbook gains a step and loses a race. docs/deployment.md currently tells the operator to claim the account before a stranger does; it will instead tell them to create the secret before first boot. The curl /api/setup check stays useful and its meaning is unchanged.

docs.title: Deployments run a published image pinned by major tag
docs.text:
Amended by ADR-0009: before 1.0, the pin is :0.Y.

Tagged releases build the prod stage and push to GHCR as ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement with 1.0.0, 1.0, 1 and latest. Both deployment paths reference that image — docker-compose.yml in place of build: ., deploy/quadlet/kendo-app.container and kendo-migrate.container in place of localhost/kendodojo:latest — and the documented pin for an operator is the major tag, :1. The image also carries the deployment bundle it needs — the compose file, the .example config, the Quadlet units, the backup scripts and setup.sh — extracted with podman run --rm <image> init | tar -x, so an operator never clones. Building from source stays supported and becomes optional.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every operator today must clone the repository and run make build before anything starts. That is the single largest barrier to a stranger self-hosting this: it requires a git checkout, a working build toolchain on the target host, and several minutes of build time before the first line of the setup instructions has any visible effect. The target operator for the quick self-host is a technical hobbyist with a VPS and a domain — not someone who wants to own a build.

A published image removes the toolchain and the build. It does not, on its own, remove the clone: the app is only half of what a host needs, and the other half is text — docker-compose.yml, .env.example, the Traefik .example files, deploy/quadlet/, deploy/bin/kendo-*.sh and the setup.sh that writes them. Publishing the image while leaving that config on the git side gives one deployment two distribution channels on two version axes, and a checkout of main against an image pinned :1 is config from the tip driving an app from 1.x.

It also raises a question the build-on-host model never had to answer: what does an operator write in their config, and what does upgrading mean?

Alembic is the real compatibility surface. The migrate service runs alembic upgrade head against the operator's live database, unattended, before app starts. An operator who pulls a new image is consenting to a schema change whether or not they realise it, and the only true rollback for a migration they did not want is a restore from backup. So the tag an operator pins is not a cosmetic preference — it is the promise the project makes about when their database will change shape under them.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
:latest only. Simplest to publish and simplest to document. Rejected because pull && up -d then drags the operator across any migration at all, including a breaking one, with no way to express "I want fixes but not a schema rewrite". The failure mode is silent and lands on the least experienced operators hardest.

Date tags (:2026-09-13). Unambiguous and trivially ordered, but a date carries no compatibility information. :2026-09-13 to :2026-10-01 tells the operator nothing about whether their data survives, so it solves publishing without solving the question publishing raises.

Semver, pinned by major (chosen). :1 means "fixes and features, no migration that requires a restore". Moving to :2 is an explicit edit the operator makes, at a time of their choosing, having read the release notes. The narrower pins (:1.0, :1.0.0) remain available for operators who want them, and :latest remains for anyone who genuinely wants the tip. Versioned documentation follows the same axis: an operator on :1 reads the 1.x docs.

The same question applies to the config, and the answers are not independent of it — whatever carries the config has to track the same axis the image is pinned on.

Clone the release branch (git clone -b release/1.x). Free in git, one line of documentation. Rejected because it keeps the clone in the install for the sake of 170 KB of text, and leaves the two axes merely conventionally aligned: nothing stops a :1 pin against a main checkout.

A release tarball asset per tag. Correct pinning, but a second artefact to publish, sign and document alongside the image.

curl … | bash bootstrap that fetches the rest at a pinned ref. Removes the clone, but adds bootstrap logic the project owns and a pipe-to-shell install.

The image carries the bundle (chosen). Podman is already the prerequisite and podman run needs no compose file, so the image can hand over its own config before anything is configured: a COPY into /bundle in the prod stage and an init branch in entrypoint.sh that tars it to stdout. Install is three commands and no git. Skew is closed by construction rather than by convention — the bundle comes out of the image it configures, so setup.sh writes that exact tag into .env rather than guessing, and there is one version axis instead of two.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Cutting a major version becomes a real commitment rather than a number.
