Any migration that cannot be rolled back by re-pointing at the previous image must land in a new major, and the release notes for it have to say what an operator must do. That discipline is the point — it is what makes :1 worth pinning — but it is a constraint on the migration chain that did not exist while every deployment built from source.

GHCR images from a private repository are not anonymously pullable and count against the account's package quota. The documented podman-compose pull path therefore cannot be exercised as a stranger experiences it until the repository is public; until then the workflow is proved by pulling with a token.

localhost/kendodojo:latest remains buildable and is still what a contributor runs. Nothing here removes the build — it stops being mandatory.

The image gains a second mode. entrypoint.sh has been deliberately narrow — one exec uvicorn, with migrations kept out of it so a failed migration never looks like an app crash — and init is the first argument it interprets. It stays a tar to stdout and nothing more: it writes no files, needs no mounts, and cannot be reached once the app is running.

The bundle becomes a shipped surface. Anything under /bundle is published to operators at that tag, so the dev-only paths (deploy/certs/, deploy/traefik/dev/) must stay out of it, and a config change now lands in a release rather than the moment it merges. setup.sh upgrade re-extracts the bundle and reports what changed instead of overwriting an operator's filled-in files.

Amended by #604: no upgrade re-extracts the bundle any more. Once installed, its files are the operator's; the upgrade is back up, pull, restart, and a release that changes a deployment file lists the change as an Operator action in its notes.

docs.title: Session Templates and Sessions stay separate tables
docs.text:
Session Templates (the recurring rule) and Sessions (one dated event) are stored as two parallel sets of three tables — session_template{,_segments,_segment_types} and session_instance{,_segments,_segment_types} — with near-identical columns. We keep all six rather than collapsing them into three tables with a discriminator column.

The resemblance is shallower than it looks, and the two have already diverged: a Session carries cancelled and the check-in window overrides, a template carries its recurrence rule (recurrence, day_of_week, recurrence_days, interval_weeks, start_date, end_date). One merged table would have to make every one of those columns nullable and trust application code to know which apply to which kind of row. The segment tables would then need a polymorphic parent — a column that points at either a template or a Session — which a foreign key cannot constrain. Six tables that each say exactly what they hold are worth more than three that need a discriminator to be read correctly.

Decided in the schema review, issue #418.

docs.title: Accounts and Members stay separate tables
docs.text:
A Member is the kendoka: name, email, date of birth, grade, emergency contact, safeguarding data. An Account is how a Member signs in: passkeys, recovery codes, Role (the code called it User / users until #436). Every Account belongs to exactly one Member — there is no sign-in without a kendoka, the first Admin included, whose Member is created when they claim the instance. Most Members have no Account. The obvious simplification is one people table; we keep two, linked by a NOT NULL, unique accounts.member_id, for three reasons.

  • They are deleted differently. Erasure hard-deletes the Account and its credentials but anonymises the Member in place, so attendance keeps a row to point at. A single table would need a tombstone row with every auth column nulled: two tables sharing one row. (Grade history is deleted on erasure, not kept: a grade and the date it was awarded can single out a kendoka even under "Deleted member", so keeping it would not be erasure — #447.)
  • They are read under different trust conditions. Accounts are looked up by the unauthenticated registration and login endpoints, where enumeration and timing parity have had real work (#239, #267, #300). Members hold the personal and under-18 data. Merging them puts that data on the row that pre-auth lookups load.
  • The roster outlives sign-ins. Most Members never sign in, and a Member who leaves loses their Account but keeps their history.

The email address is stored once, on the Member, and is both the contact address and the sign-in identifier: two copies that must always be equal is one copy. Pre-auth code therefore finds an Account by joining its Member on that one indexed column — it matches on members.email and loads only the Account, never the Member row, so the trust boundary above still holds. Only an Admin can change the address; the app sends no mail, so a self-service change could not be verified.

Decided in the schema review, issue #418.

docs.title: The app connects as a least-privilege database user
docs.text:
The official PostgreSQL image makes POSTGRES_USER (kendo) a superuser, and every process used to connect as it — including the internet-facing web app. A compromised app (SQL injection, code execution in its container) could then run shell commands in the database container with COPY … TO PROGRAM, read and write server files, drop the schema, and create users. The app needs none of that: it never changes the schema at runtime. So the web app and app/cli.py connect as a second database user that can only read and write rows, and kendo stays the superuser for migrations, backup and restore. The goal is to contain a compromised app, not to hide data from it: the app user still reads and writes every app table.

  • Two URLs. DATABASE_URL is the app user's login everywhere; a new MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL holds the superuser login and is given only to the migration step, so the superuser password never reaches the app container.
  • The migration step maintains the app user. app/db/bootstrap.py already runs as superuser before every app start. After alembic upgrade head it creates the user named in DATABASE_URL if missing, sets its password from the secret, and re-applies the grants, on every run: existing volumes are covered, drift is repaired, and rotating the password is changing the secret.
  • Grants: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on app tables, USAGE, SELECT on sequences, SELECT only on alembic_version (so a compromised app cannot fake the schema version), set as default privileges for tables kendo creates later. No TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, REFERENCES or CREATE. No TEMP either: it comes through PUBLIC, so it is revoked from PUBLIC (#482).
  • No sliding back. The app refuses to start when connected as a superuser, and the e2e tests run the server as the app user, so a missing grant fails in CI rather than tempting someone to point DATABASE_URL back at kendo.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• A third user owning the schema, non-superuser, for migrations, leaving the superuser to backup and restore only. Rejected for now: the migration step is short-lived and on the backend network only, while moving ownership off the bootstrap superuser cannot be done with REASSIGN OWNED and means altering every object. The internet-facing app was the risk worth paying for.
  • Creating the app user in a docker-entrypoint-initdb.d script. Rejected: it runs only on an empty volume, so existing volumes miss it and a password change becomes a manual ALTER ROLE.
  • Grants in an Alembic migration. Rejected: the password is a secret and cannot live in the chain, so user creation would be split across two places.

Decided in issue #453.

docs.title: Auth Sessions are opaque server-side rows, not JWTs
docs.text:
Auth Sessions used to be stateless HS256 JWTs carrying role and is_active, re-read from the database only at renewal. Nothing could revoke one: a stolen cookie lived out its 7-day ceiling, a demotion took up to half a token life to bite, and logout only cleared the cookie. Worse, a leaked JWT_SECRET let an attacker mint an Auth Session for any Account, or a recovery token, which is enough to enrol their own passkey on it and keep it.

Now every Auth Session is a row in auth_sessions. The table is not called sessions, because a Session is a training event. The cookie carries a random id (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)) and the table stores only its SHA-256, so a database dump or backup yields no live Auth Session. The guard looks the row up on every authenticated request and joins the Account and its Member, so role and whether the Member may sign in always come from the database.

  • Revocation is deleting rows, and the foreign keys do most of it. Logout deletes the row; "sign out everywhere" deletes all of the Account's rows, the current one included. account_id is ON DELETE CASCADE, so erasure revokes with no code. Each row records the passkey it signed in with (passkey_id, nullable, ON DELETE CASCADE), so removing a lost device's passkey ends that device's Auth Sessions. A demotion needs no revocation hook: the next request reads the new row. Archiving or suspending is refused the same way, and also deletes the Account's rows (see the #484 amendment).
  • Recovery tokens are rows too, with a kind of recovery and a 15-minute life, still sent as a Bearer header and refused in the cookie. They are single-use: the row is deleted once the new passkey is enrolled. Redeeming one does not revoke the Account's other Auth Sessions; "sign out everywhere" is the tool for that. This removes the last JWT, so joserfc goes. JWT_SECRET stays, because it also keys the HMAC behind the decoy user ids in webauthn_ceremony.py, but leaking it no longer grants access. It and JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES keep their names: they are deployment surface, and renaming them is not worth breaking every instance's env file.
  • Lifetime is unchanged: 8 hours idle, 7 days absolute. expires_at slides forward once an Auth Session is past the halfway mark of its idle window, not on every request. The cookie's max_age is the absolute ceiling and is set once, at sign-in; the server enforces the idle window. The cookie is never re-set mid-session, so SessionRenewalMiddleware and its logout race go away. The slide is written in the guard, before the route runs, and most guarded routes are reads that never commit, so SqlAuthSessionRepository.slide commits itself: the one repository that does, and safe only because nothing else is pending at that point. The cost of a cookie set only once is that it can outlive its idle-expired row, which is the stale cookie #397 fixed: accepted, because the id it carries is refused and the SPA routes to /login on the 401.
  • Expired rows are deleted at sign-in, in one indexed statement, and refused when read. There is no scheduler.
  • "Sign out everywhere" is the Account's own. An Admin version waits for a deactivate action to exist.
  • No Auth Session list on the profile. Naming a device means storing a User-Agent and IP: personal data that erasure would have to cover, for a feature "sign out everywhere" already covers.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• Keep the JWT and add a jti checked against a table. Rejected: once every request reads the table, the signature proves nothing the row doesn't, and a leaked JWT_SECRET would still forge recovery tokens.
  • Keep role and active status in the token, and delete Auth Sessions when they change. Rejected: every future write to either needs a matching revocation call, and missing one is a silent privilege bug. The per-request read is one indexed join.
  • Removing any passkey revokes all the Account's other Auth Sessions. Rejected: the passkey_id foreign key ends exactly the lost device's sessions, with no code.
  • Clean up expired rows in the migrate step. Rejected: it runs only when the app restarts, which a long-running instance rarely does.

Deploying this signs everyone out once: existing JWT cookies have no row.

Decided in issue #455.

Amended by #484: whether an Account may sign in is its Member's Membership Status, not an Account flag. archived and suspended are refused at sign-in, recovery, passkey enrolment and on every authenticated request (401, as for no Auth Session); inactive keeps access. The members domain owns the rule (BARRED_FROM_SIGN_IN in app.members.db_models, and MAY_SIGN_IN, the same rule as one SQL predicate), and auth reads it only through the app.auth.member_directory port (ADR-0006). The Auth Session join reads MAY_SIGN_IN in its one statement. accounts.is_active, which nothing ever set false, is dropped.

Barring a Member also deletes every Auth Session row of their Account, of both kinds, in the same transaction as the status change. The per-request refusal alone left the rows in place, so an Admin reinstating the Member before they expired revived them: a session the Member, or whoever held their cookie, had when they were barred came back with no new sign-in. The refusal stays the guarantee while the bar lasts; the deletion makes the bar final for every session that predates it. This is the one place a status change revokes, and it does not reopen the rejected "delete Auth Sessions when they change" option: missing the call would only bring back the revival, never let a barred Member in.

docs.title: Before 1.0, releases pin by minor, not major
docs.text: The project goes public on 0.x, not 1.0.0. Until 1.0, 0.Y stands in for the major in ADR-0004's promise: a Breaking change bumps Y, everything else (fixes and features alike) bumps the patch, and the documented operator pin is :0.Y. Docs publish as 0.Y.x. From 1.0.0 on, ADR-0004's major pin (:1) applies unchanged. This amends ADR-0004's pin rule; it does not replace it.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0004 makes the pinned tag a promise about when an operator's database and configuration change shape under them. In SemVer the major is always 0 before 1.0, so a :0 pin promises nothing: every breaking change in the 0.x series would reach an operator on pull && up -d. The release workflow and the docs versioning both derive the pin from the major alone, which is right for 1.x and wrong for 0.x.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
Start at 1.0.0. Keeps ADR-0004 exactly as written. Rejected: going public invites contributors and the first outside operators, and the project wants room to make breaking changes while that settles, without spending a major number on each.

0.x pinned by major (:0). No workflow change. Rejected: it is the :latest failure ADR-0004 already rejected, under a different name.

0.x pinned by minor (chosen). The common pre-1.0 reading of SemVer. Features go in the patch, not the minor, so the only reason Y moves is a Breaking change and :0.Y means exactly what :1 will mean later.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The release workflow's pin and the docs version are computed from major.minor while the major is 0, and from the major alone afterwards. Both must switch at 1.0 without anyone remembering to edit them.

Only the latest 0.Y is supported. A security fix ships as a patch on it, even when it has to break; such a release says so under a Security heading, and the upgrade refuses to run until the operator has acted, rather than degrading silently.

In 0.x a Breaking change may rename or remove a setting outright, provided the upgrade stops hard on the old one. From 1.0 a rename keeps accepting the old name with a warning until the next major.

There is no exit criterion for 1.0 yet. Without one, 0.x has no natural end; deciding it is deferred, not forgotten.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Podman + podman-compose (Docker Compose may work — see Container runtime)
  • uv — uv sync in backend/ builds .venv from uv.lock (fetching Python 3.13 if needed)
  • Node 22

docs.title: Get the code
docs.text:
Operators do not need a clone — the release image carries its own deployment bundle (Quick self-host). Contributors do:

git clone https://github.com/booji/KendoDojoManagement.git
cd KendoDojoManagement

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Copy the dev env file (safe to commit — contains no real secrets): 

cp .env.dev .env.dev.local   # optional local overrides

No edits needed to get started, but the backend container does not load .env.dev (only db does): its settings are interpolated from it, which needs --env-file .env.dev on every Compose command. make dev passes it; a bare podman-compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up starts the backend with JWT_SECRET, SETUP_TOKEN and the rest blank (#483).

docs.title: Start the dev stack
docs.text:
make dev

This starts: - proxy — Traefik, on host ports 8443 (HTTPS) and 8080 (redirect to 8443) - backend — FastAPI with hot-reload on file changes, on host port 8000 - frontend — Vite dev server with HMR, on host port 5173 - db — PostgreSQL 16, published on host port 5433

Open https://dojo.localhost:8443. Browsers resolve *.localhost to loopback, so no /etc/hosts entry is needed, and treat it as a secure context. Traefik routes /api, /health and /static to the backend and everything else to Vite, so the browser sits on one origin for both the UI and the API — the same shape production has (see docs/adr/0001-single-origin-api-under-api-prefix.md).

The proxy is not decoration. .env.dev sets COOKIE_SECURE=true, TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true and a real WEBAUTHN_RP_ID/WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, so Secure cookies, passkey ceremonies and the X-Forwarded-For path that rate limiting and lockout depend on are exercised here rather than for the first time in production — the reasoning is in docs/adr/0002-traefik-in-the-dev-stack.md.

http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:8000 stay published as an escape hatch for when a certificate is missing or HMR misbehaves through the proxy. On those, cookies are not sent (they are Secure) and X-Forwarded-For is whatever the caller claims — so do not test login or rate limiting there.

Vite's websocket setting is server-wide, so exactly one of the two origins gets working HMR — the proxy by default. To hand it to :5173 instead, start the stack with the proxy origin emptied:

DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN= make dev

Then :5173 live-reloads and https://dojo.localhost:8443 does not (the page still works; changes need a refresh). Put DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN= in .env.dev to make it stick across runs.

docs.title: The dev TLS certificate
docs.text:
The certificate is on the critical path: .env.dev sets COOKIE_SECURE=true, and browsers refuse WebAuthn on a page with a certificate error — so a degraded certificate looks like a perfectly healthy stack right up until the first login or passkey ceremony fails.

1. Generate. make dev runs make certs for you, or run it directly:

make certs         # issue if missing, untrusted, or no longer covering dojo.localhost
make certs-force   # reissue unconditionally (no manual `rm` needed)

It says which generator it used. With mkcert on your PATH the pair is issued by your local CA; without it you get a self-signed pair and a warning saying so. Install mkcert and re-run make certs — it notices the self-signed certificate and reissues. The pair lives in deploy/certs/ and is gitignored: per-machine, never committed.

2. Trust the CA — on the machine the browser runs on. mkcert -install installs the CA into the trust store of the OS it runs on. If the stack and the browser are on different systems, a successful-looking install does nothing for the browser:

Stack runs on Browser runs on Install the CA where Linux (native) the same Linux mkcert -install in that shell WSL2 Windows export $(mkcert -CAROOT)/rootCA.pem from WSL and import it into the Windows store (certutil -addstore -user Root rootCA.pem), or install mkcert on Windows and run mkcert -install there A VM or remote dev box your laptop copy rootCA.pem off the box and import it into the laptop's store

Firefox keeps its own store. It does not read the OS trust store. Either install nss-tools (certutil) before mkcert -install so mkcert can add the CA to Firefox's NSS database, or on Windows set security.enterprise_roots.enabled to true in about:config.

3. Verify. Open https://dojo.localhost:8443 — no warning, and a padlock. That is the whole check; a warning means the browser does not trust the CA, not that the certificate is malformed.

4. Restart the proxy after any reissue. Traefik loads the certificate at startup and its file provider watches the config files, not the certificate bytes. A replaced pair is not picked up until the proxy restarts (make down && make dev), which otherwise looks exactly like the new certificate not working.

When it goes wrong:

Symptom Cause Fix Passkey ceremony fails, everything else looks fine self-signed certificate install mkcert, make certs mkcert -install succeeded but the browser still warns CA is in the wrong OS's trust store see the table above Chrome is happy, Firefox is not Firefox's separate NSS store nss-tools + mkcert -install, or security.enterprise_roots.enabled The old warning persists after reissuing Traefik still serving the startup certificate make down && make dev

If you need to get in without a certificate at all, http://localhost:5173 is still published — but cookies and passkeys do not work there, and HMR only reaches it if the stack was started with DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN= (above).

docs.title: Network layout
docs.text:
Two networks, mirroring the Quadlet production deployment in deploy/quadlet (kendo-edge + kendo-backend):

Network Members Purpose edge proxy, frontend, backend Traefik fronts both; carries the published host ports backend backend, db The only path to PostgreSQL

frontend is not on the backend network. It runs arbitrary npm dependencies with node_modules mounted — the least trusted container in the stack — so it cannot reach the database at all.

Nothing uses network_mode: host any more. Host-networked containers join no Compose network, so there was nothing to segment, and the database ended up binding host port 5432 directly (see below). The browser runs on the host and never joins a Compose network, so browser reachability depends only on published ports: 8443/8080 for the proxy, and the 1:1 5173:5173 and 8000:8000 escape hatches behind it.

Two runtime quirks are worth knowing, both verified on podman 5.6.0:

  • isolate=true is what actually enforces the split. Podman's bridge networks are otherwise mutually routable by IP — the frontend cannot resolve db, but it can open a socket to the database's 10.89.x.x address. The driver_opts in both Compose files close that. Docker isolates user-defined bridges natively, so the option is redundant there — and untested, like everything else on Docker. If a Docker version rejects the driver_opts key, dropping it loses nothing on that runtime.
  • The backend network is not internal: true, unlike Internal=true on kendo-backend.network in deploy/quadlet. Podman disables DNS on internal networks (dnsname and internal networks are incompatible), so the service name db stops resolving and the backend cannot connect. The trade is the database's outbound route, which cannot be removed on Podman without also losing service-name DNS.

docs.title: Why the database is on 5433, not 5432
docs.text:
db publishes a mapped port rather than binding the host's. Host networking used to make it bind host port 5432 directly — the conventional PostgreSQL port. Anything else on the machine holding that port (a system install, another project's stack, a leftover container) claimed it first, and the dev database then exited 1 while podman-compose up -d db still reported success. A published port fails loudly on a collision, and 5433 avoids the common one entirely.

To run two checkouts of this repo side by side, set a different POSTGRES_PORT in .env.dev and change the port in both database URLs in the same file to match. The other four host ports are fixed and will collide: 8443 and 8080 (proxy), 5173 (Vite) and 8000 (uvicorn). Only one checkout's dev stack can be up at a time unless you edit them — and 8443 also appears in WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, CORS_ORIGINS, the dev routing file and server.hmr.clientPort. The frontend port must stay mapped 1:1 (5173:5173): Vite's HMR client infers the websocket port from the browser's location, so publishing it on a different host port needs server.hmr.clientPort set in frontend/vite.config.ts.

docs.title: Connecting from the host
docs.text:
The port is published on 127.0.0.1 only — the dev credentials are weak and committed to the repo, so the database is deliberately not reachable from the LAN. Host-side tooling (alembic, psql, a one-off script) must point at the published port, not 5432, and address 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost (which can resolve to ::1, where nothing is listening):

export DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://kendo_dev:kendo_dev_password@127.0.0.1:5433/kendo_dev
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U kendo_dev -d kendo_dev

That is the superuser, MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL in .env.dev, which alembic needs. The backend itself connects as the restricted kendo_app user that the migrate service creates, and refuses to start as a superuser (ADR-0007). After adding a migration, make migrate runs that service again.

If you get password authentication failed for user "kendo_dev" on port 5432, you are talking to a different PostgreSQL — the credentials are not the problem, the port is.

docs.title: Make targets
docs.text:
Target What it does make List the targets (starts nothing) make dev Start the hot-reload dev stack make test Start the test watcher (re-runs pytest on every save) make screenshots Regenerate the README / docs sessions screenshots (docs/assets, desktop and mobile, light and dark) from a made-up dojo — rerun after a UI change to the calendar make build Build the production image as localhost/kendodojo:latest (releases run the published image — see ADR-0004) make down Stop the stacks this checkout starts — dev and test make down-selfhost Stop the quick self-host stack — takes the dojo offline make certs Issue the dojo.localhost dev TLS certificate if it is missing or untrusted (run for you by make dev) make certs-force Reissue the dev TLS certificate unconditionally make logs Tail dev service logs make migrate Run alembic upgrade head on the dev database as the superuser and re-provision the app user make help List all targets

The Makefile auto-detects podman-compose vs docker compose, so the targets run under either. That detection is kept because it costs nothing, not because Docker is tested — see Container runtime.

make down deliberately leaves the quick self-host alone: on a machine that is actually serving a dojo, stopping it must be a deliberate act, so it has its own target. The same reasoning already governs make clean refusing to remove the production database volume.

make dev generates a per-machine dojo.localhost certificate under deploy/certs/ (gitignored) if one is missing, self-signed while mkcert is available, or no longer covering the dev host. The full step — generate, trust, verify, reissue, and the failure modes — is The dev TLS certificate.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Maintainer steps. The decisions behind them are ADR-0004 and ADR-0009; the contributor side is CONTRIBUTING.md.

The branches follow git-flow:

Branch Holds Merges into develop the next release; the default branch. Feature PRs are squash-merged here. — release/X.Y.Z one release being prepared, cut from develop; carries the rc tags main, by merge commit hotfix/X.Y.Z an urgent fix, cut from main main, by merge commit main released code only; every release tag is on it develop, after each release

Release when ready; a hotfix goes out at once.

docs.title: Pick the version
docs.text:
List what develop has that main does not, and look for the breaking label:

git fetch origin
git log --oneline origin/main..origin/develop
gh pr list --base develop --state merged --label breaking --search "merged:>=$(git log -1 --format=%cs origin/main)"
  • Any merged PR labelled breaking → bump Y and reset the patch: 0.1.4 → 0.2.0. This starts a new Release line.
  • Otherwise, features and fixes alike → bump the patch Z: 0.1.4 → 0.1.5.

From 1.0 the same rule bumps the major instead of Y.

docs.title: Cut the release branch
docs.text:
git switch -c release/X.Y.Z origin/develop

On a new Release line only, move the deployment bundle and the operator docs to its pin in this branch, so the image and the docs published for the line show it. Start with RELEASE_PIN in backend/tests/deploy_contract.py, then list every mention of the old pin (here 0.1) and update each, along with the next line the comments name as the one to move to:

git grep -n -e ':0\.1\b' -e '0\.1\.x' -- README.md docs mkdocs.yml \
  setup.sh entrypoint.sh docker-compose.yml .env.example deploy

The backend tests then fail on any shipped file or page that still names a different image pin, and the release workflow refuses to push a release tag whose pin the bundle and the docs do not name.

Then write the upgrade notes. In Upgrading, add an "Upgrading to X.Y" section and copy into it the Operator action section of every breaking PR in the release, under Compose and Quadlet headings as each applies. Replace the "None yet" line on the first one. A patch release needs no upgrading section.

Commit those to the release branch and push it.

docs.title: Collect the Operator actions
docs.text:
Every release, patch or not. No upgrade step overwrites a deployment file (#604), so a change to one reaches an operator only through the release notes. Collect the Operator action section of every PR in the release that has one, breaking or not. Then check that every commit touching a deployment file came with one:

git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD -- deploy docker-compose.yml .env.example setup.sh

A PR missing its section gets one written now, from its diff. Keep the collected actions for the release notes (Release, step 3), under a Compose heading and a Quadlet heading.

docs.title: Rehearse a release candidate
docs.text:
First refresh the bundled FIK affiliate list, which every instance syncs into its Federation catalogue on upgrade. From backend/ on the release branch:

uv run python -m scripts.update_fik_affiliates

It rewrites backend/app/federations/fik_affiliates.json from https://www.kendo-fik.org/organization/affiliate, or fails without writing if the page's layout has changed. Review the diff and land any change through a PR like any other fix; a new country heading fails the run until it is added to the script's ISO table.

An affiliate that drops off the list is deactivated on upgrade, not deleted. One that later returns to the list stays inactive until an Admin re-activates it in Admin Settings: the Admin owns is_active, so the sync never turns it back on.

Then tag the release branch and push the tag:

git tag -a vX.Y.Z-rc1 -m vX.Y.Z-rc1
git push origin vX.Y.Z-rc1

An rc tag runs the full suite (tests.yml) and publishes an image under its exact tag only, never the moving tags operators pin, and its docs publish nowhere.

The Release image's GHCR package must be public, or every operator's anonymous pull fails with unauthorized. A package is created private on its first push, and GitHub has no API to change that: if the package was ever recreated, make it public under its Package settings. Check with an anonymous pull before rehearsing, from the clean host (never logged in to ghcr.io):

podman pull ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:$RC_TAG   # e.g. RC_TAG=X.Y.Z-rc1

Rehearse on a clean host: install from the rc image with Quick self-host. Then upgrade a host running the previous release to it, the way an operator pins a Version (Upgrading § Pinning a Version): apply the collected Operator actions, edit the pin to the rc tag, and run the routine upgrade. The pin is Image= in kendo-app.container, kendo-migrate.container and kendo-ip-retention.container on Quadlet, and KENDO_IMAGE in .env on Compose. Do not retag the rc image as :0.1: the rehearsal would then skip the pin edit an operator makes. Rehearse the rollback too, by editing the pin back to the previous release and restoring the backup the upgrade took.

A fix found here goes on the release branch, and the next rc is -rc2.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
1. Open a PR from release/X.Y.Z into main. Merge it with a merge commit, not a squash: main must contain the commits develop already has, or the back-merge conflicts.

  2. Tag the merge commit on main and push the tag:

    git fetch origin && git switch main && git merge --ff-only origin/main
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z

    The tag publishes the image as X.Y.Z, X.Y and latest, plus X from 1.0 on, and the docs for its Release line: 0.Y.x before 1.0, X.x after.

  3. Publish the GitHub release from the tag with generated notes; they are grouped by label, breaking first. Put the Operator actions you collected above them, under an Operator action heading with Compose and Quadlet subheadings, or write "None" there. On a new Release line, also link the upgrading section.

  4. Merge main back into develop with a PR (merge commit), so the release branch's commits reach develop. Open it from a copy of main, so the repository's "automatically delete head branches" setting removes the copy on merge:

    git push origin origin/main:refs/heads/chore/backmerge-X.Y.Z
gh pr create --base develop --head chore/backmerge-X.Y.Z

A back-merge from the release branch during the rc phase works the same way, from a copy of release/X.Y.Z. 5. Delete release/X.Y.Z by hand, with git push origin --delete release/X.Y.Z. The ruleset blocks deletion of release branches, so auto-delete skips the branch after the merge in step 1. The maintainer's bypass allows this deletion.

docs.title: Hotfix
docs.text:
A fix that cannot wait for develop, usually a security fix:

  1. git switch -c hotfix/X.Y.Z origin/main, with Z one above the latest release.
  2. Fix it there and open a PR into main. The PR runs the full suite; rehearse an rc as above if there is time.
  3. Merge with a merge commit, tag vX.Y.Z on main, and publish the release exactly as in Release, back-merge into develop included.

A security fix that has to break ships as a patch all the same, with its operator action under a Security heading in the release notes and in Upgrading; see SECURITY.md.

docs.title: TDD workflow
docs.text: The working agreements live in CLAUDE.md, which people and coding agents follow alike. These are its design and testing sections, included here as written.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Deep modules (Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design): favor small interfaces hiding large implementations. A caller should need to know as little as possible about what's underneath. New modules and abstractions should earn their existence by hiding meaningful complexity.

Abstraction is encouraged where it genuinely aids human readability; avoid speculative abstractions for hypothetical future needs.

docs.title: TDD Workflow
docs.text:
Follow red-green as vertical slices, not horizontal slicing: 1. Write one failing test for the next small behavior. 2. Write the minimum implementation to make it pass. 3. Refactor if needed, then move to the next test.

Never write a full test suite first and then implement everything — that is horizontal slicing and is explicitly not the workflow here.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
make test

This mounts ./backend into a container alongside an ephemeral PostgreSQL instance and re-runs the full suite on every file change. The database is destroyed on make down.

One-shot run inside the running container: 

podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml exec test pytest -q

A one-shot run of the whole suite, with optional pytest flags: 

podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm test
podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm -e PYTEST_ARGS=-x test
podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm \
  -e PYTEST_TARGET=tests/test_members.py test

Pass pytest flags through PYTEST_ARGS, not positionally after the service name: podman-compose treats trailing arguments as the container command, so run --rm test -x fails with crun: executable file `-x` not found in $PATH. Only real docker compose forwards them. Both variables interpolate unquoted, so keep values free of *, ? and [].

docs.title: Backups (as kendo)
docs.text:
Nightly backup to ~/backups, keeping the newest 14 of each artefact, driven by a systemd user timer. Each run writes two files sharing one timestamp:

File Contents kendo-<stamp>.dump Postgres, pg_dump custom format kendo-uploads-<stamp>.tar the kendo-app-uploads volume — logos and login backgrounds

Uploaded images live on a volume, not in the database, so the dump alone does not cover them. With a backup key set, both are encrypted and end in .age: kendo-<stamp>.dump.age, kendo-uploads-<stamp>.tar.age.

The Quick self-host (Compose) stack has no nightly timer. It takes a backup to ~/backups on every ./setup.sh upgrade, and the backup key and off-site settings below apply to it too — run ./setup.sh backup-key without --quadlet.

./setup.sh --quadlet installs kendo-backup.service and kendo-backup.timer in ~/.config/systemd/user/ and enables the timer: the first backup runs at the timer's next OnCalendar= (02:30 as shipped). Without setup.sh, the same by hand:

cp deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.service ~/.config/systemd/user/
cp deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.timer   ~/.config/systemd/user/
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now kendo-backup.timer

Either way, check the schedule and take one now:

systemctl --user list-timers kendo-backup.timer --no-pager
systemctl --user start kendo-backup.service
ls -lh ~/backups

./setup.sh check --quadlet warns when backups are not encrypted, when an off-site copy is not set up or would be refused, when the newest backup is two or more days old, and when the last run failed — including a failed off-site copy, which leaves the local backup fresh.

docs.title: The backup key
docs.text:
Backups hold every Member's personal data, including under-18 and safeguarding data, so they are encrypted with age. Install offers to set a key; to set one later, or replace one, run from the deployment bundle:

sudo dnf install -y age   # or: sudo apt install -y age
./setup.sh backup-key --quadlet

It shows the private key — one AGE-SECRET-KEY-1… line — once, and asks you to type its last 6 characters back to show it is saved. Only the public half is kept on the host, as KENDO_BACKUP_RECIPIENT in ~/.config/kendo/backup.env. That is the point: nothing on the host can read a backup back, so neither can anyone who breaks into it.

It also means losing the key loses the backups. Nobody can decrypt a backup without the key it was made under — not the project, not the host, not you. The live database is unaffected; what you lose is the ability to restore.

With no key set, backups are still written, unencrypted, with a warning on every run. No backup would be worse.

docs.title: Keeping the key
docs.text:
• Keep it in two places, e.g. the club's password manager plus a printed copy with the club records.
  • Save it with its start date, e.g. "Kendo backup key (from 2026-10-06)". A backup's filename carries its date, so the date shows which key opens it after a change.
  • When a volunteer leaves, the key is handed over, not lost. If they kept a copy, change it.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
Destructive — stops writes, drops and recreates the database:

systemctl --user stop kendo-app
# Second argument is optional; pass the uploads tarball with the same timestamp
# to restore logos and backgrounds alongside the database.
~/.local/bin/kendo-restore.sh \
  ~/backups/kendo-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.dump.age \
  ~/backups/kendo-uploads-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.tar.age
systemctl --user restart kendo-migrate kendo-app
# Stopping kendo-app stopped Traefik too, which needs it (Requires=); restarting
# the app does not bring it back, so start it (#628).
systemctl --user start kendo-traefik

On the Compose stack, from the install directory. Its database container and uploads volume are project-scoped, so name them (a failed setup.sh upgrade prints this command with them filled in):

podman-compose stop app
KENDO_DB_CONTAINER=$(podman ps -a --format '{{.Names}}' \
    --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=kendodojo \
    --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=db) \
KENDO_UPLOADS_VOLUME=kendodojo_static_uploads \
  bash deploy/bin/kendo-restore.sh \
  ~/backups/kendo-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.dump.age \
  ~/backups/kendo-uploads-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.tar.age
podman-compose up -d --force-recreate

Both end by re-running migrate, as the restore prints when it finishes: the app's database user has no grants until it does (#481).

Plaintext backups (.dump, .tar, from before a key was set) restore with the same command.

For an encrypted backup it asks for the key at a hidden prompt: paste the whole AGE-SECRET-KEY-1… line. This works inside sudo machinectl shell kendo@ /bin/bash. The key is never written to disk, and neither is anything it decrypts — it streams straight into pg_restore and the uploads volume.

The key is checked against every file before anything is changed, so a wrong key leaves the database untouched:

  • "This backup was encrypted with a different key" — keys were changed since. Use the one that was active on the date in the filename.
  • "That is not a valid backup key" — the paste is incomplete. Paste the whole line, exactly as saved.

docs.title: Restore drill
docs.text:
Check that the backups you have actually open, without touching the server. On any machine with age and the PostgreSQL client tools, with the key saved to key.txt:

age -d -i key.txt kendo-<stamp>.dump.age | pg_restore --list | head
age -d -i key.txt kendo-uploads-<stamp>.tar.age | tar -t | head
rm key.txt

A table of contents and a list of files mean the backup is good. Nothing decrypted is written to disk; only key.txt is, so delete it afterwards.

Run it now and then — monthly, say — against the newest off-site copy, not the one on the host. One drill shows that backups are still being made, that they reach the remote, and that the key still opens them. Nothing reminds you; put it in the club calendar.

docs.title: Lost or leaked key
docs.text:
A new key can be set at any time with ./setup.sh backup-key --quadlet. It runs the same save-and-confirm as install, takes a backup under the new key at once, then lists the older backups and offers to delete them.

Only backups made from then on use the new key. Older ones still open only with the old key — that cannot be worked around, or an attacker could do it too.

  • Lost (nobody has the key any more): set a new key. The older backups can no longer be opened; delete them, or let them age out — 14 runs on the host, and KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS off-site.
  • Leaked (someone else may have it — a volunteer left on bad terms, a printed copy went missing, the password manager was breached): set a new key and delete the older backups everywhere. Off-site, that includes emptying the provider's trash or recycle bin, or the files stay readable there for another 30 days or so.

docs.title: Off-site copies (optional)
docs.text:
A backup on the host does not survive losing the host — an old PC, a Raspberry Pi, a cheap VPS. Each run can copy its encrypted files to storage the club already has, with rclone. Add to ~/.config/kendo/backup.env — an rclone remote, then a folder, and optionally how long to keep copies:

KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE=gdrive:kendo-backups
KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS=90
  • Encrypted (.age) files from the last 7 days that the remote does not have yet are copied, so a copy that failed one night goes up with the next. Plaintext never leaves the host: with no backup key, the copy is skipped and the log says why, and plaintext backups from before the key are never copied.
  • KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS deletes kendo-*.age files older than that many days, in that folder only. About 90 is a good value: it also limits how long an erased Member's data survives in backups. Leave it unset if the credential cannot delete (see below).
  • If the copy fails, the local backup is kept, the run shows as failed in systemctl --user status kendo-backup (as kendo), and ./setup.sh upgrade carries on regardless. The reason is in the unit's log, read from your admin account: sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-backup.service --no-pager (Deployment § Logs).
  • Each rclone call is stopped after an hour, so a stalled upload cannot block the next night's backup. On a slow link, raise it with KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_TIMEOUT=2h (or 30m, 90s).

rclone runs as kendo, with kendo's own config. Install it and add a remote from a machinectl shell:

sudo dnf install -y rclone   # or: sudo apt install -y rclone
sudo machinectl shell kendo@ /bin/bash
rclone config

The host has no browser, so the login is done on a laptop: answer n to "Use auto config?", run the rclone authorize … command it prints on a laptop with rclone installed, and paste the token back. Details: rclone remote setup.

Then check it works after the next backup:

systemctl --user start kendo-backup.service
rclone lsf gdrive:kendo-backups

docs.title: Keep the credential's reach small
docs.text:
The rclone credential lives on the host. Whoever controls the host can do anything that credential can, so give it the backups and nothing else:

  • Google Drive: scope = drive.file (below) — rclone sees only the files it created, so the club's other Drive files are out of reach.
  • OneDrive: rclone has no setting that narrows it; the token reaches the whole OneDrive, including files shared with that account. Use a separate Microsoft account that holds only the backups.
  • B2 or S3-compatible storage: a key limited to one bucket (and a name prefix), with no delete permission. Expire old copies with the bucket's lifecycle rule, and leave KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS unset.
  • Hetzner Storage Box: a sub-account limited to one directory.
  • SFTP to a NAS: a dedicated user confined to one folder.
  • Any provider: an account that holds nothing but the backups. Keep its login in the club password manager, next to the backup key.

docs.title: What the trash protects, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
Google Drive and OneDrive cannot issue a credential without delete rights. Deletes made the normal way — including KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS expiry — go to the trash or recycle bin, which keeps them for about 30 days. That catches mistakes. It does not stop someone who has taken over the host: the same credential can delete permanently, skipping the trash.

So on Drive and OneDrive, someone who has taken over the host can delete the off-site copies along with the host's own. For a club that is usually an acceptable risk — the backups are encrypted, so a breach cannot read them, only destroy them. If it is not acceptable for yours, use a credential without delete rights (B2 above, or storage with object lock or snapshots), or have another machine pull the backups instead.

Expired copies also sit in the trash for those 30 days, so an erased Member's data can outlive KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS by that long.

docs.title: Google Drive
docs.text:
In rclone config: storage type drive, and at the scope question choose drive.file. Name the remote gdrive, then:

KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE=gdrive:kendo-backups
KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS=90

Log in with rclone authorize "drive" on the laptop. If transfers are slow or fail with rate-limit errors, rclone's shared client ID is busy; rclone's Drive page shows how to make your own.

docs.title: OneDrive
docs.text:
Ideally under a Microsoft account used only for the backups (see above). In rclone config: storage type onedrive, name the remote onedrive, then:

KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE=onedrive:kendo-backups
KENDO_BACKUP_REMOTE_KEEP_DAYS=90

Log in with rclone authorize "onedrive" on the laptop. Personal versus business accounts, scopes, and Microsoft 365 admin approval are covered on rclone's OneDrive page.

docs.title: Other storage
docs.text:
Anything rclone supports works — the files are already encrypted, so the storage need not be trusted with member data. See rclone's provider list.

  • Backblaze B2: a bucket-scoped key without delete permission, plus a lifecycle rule. The strongest option here.
  • Cloudflare R2: S3-compatible, with no charge for downloading a backup to restore.
  • Hetzner Storage Box: SFTP, with a sub-account per directory and its own snapshots.
  • SFTP to a NAS: best with the NAS's snapshots turned on.
  • Avoid Wasabi: it bills a 1 TB minimum and charges each object for 90 days, however briefly it is kept.

docs.title: Pulling instead of pushing
docs.text: A NAS or another always-on machine can pull the encrypted backups from ~/backups on its own schedule, instead of the host pushing them. The host then holds no credential that can reach the copies. How to set that up depends on the machine and is not covered here. ./setup.sh check will still warn that no off-site copy is configured, because the host cannot see the pull.

docs.title: The disk itself
docs.text: Encrypted backups do not protect the live database or the uploads volume on the host's disk. Full-disk encryption on the host (LUKS, or your cloud provider's encrypted volumes) covers a stolen disk or a decommissioned drive: see Encrypt the disk.

docs.title: Quick self-host
docs.text:
This is a supported production path for a single dojo: one host, Traefik terminating TLS with a Let's Encrypt certificate, three commands.

Outgrowing it? The Hardened deployment is what you graduate to — the same setup.sh, run as ./setup.sh --quadlet, adds systemd units, Podman secrets, network segmentation and automated backups.

1. Get the deployment files:

The release image carries the files a deployment needs — this compose file, the .example config, the Quadlet units, the backup scripts and setup.sh — so there is no clone and no build (ADR-0004):

podman run --rm ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:0.1 init | tar -x

(Working from a checkout instead? Skip that — the files are already here.)

2. Configure it:

./setup.sh

It asks for your domain and an ACME email, generates POSTGRES_PASSWORD, JWT_SECRET, SETUP_TOKEN and the app's own database password — the app connects as kendo_app, which can only read and write rows, and the superuser login goes to the migrate service alone — and writes .env, kendo-app.env, deploy/traefik/selfhost/traefik.yml and dynamic/kendo.yml from their .example files.

The configuration is split in two, the same way as on the hardened deployment:

  • kendo-app.env holds every app setting: the domain values, session timeouts, the timing floors, TZ and so on. It is written from deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example, the file the Quadlet deployment uses too, and holds no secret. The app and migrate services read the whole file, so a setting a release adds there reaches the app without a change to docker-compose.yml. Tune the app here.
  • .env holds only what docker-compose.yml itself interpolates — the image pin KENDO_IMAGE, the db's TZ and POSTGRES_* — plus the superuser login MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL and the app's secrets (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, SETUP_TOKEN). No container reads it whole, which is what keeps the superuser password away from the app (ADR-0007).

The secrets reach the containers as files in secrets/, which setup.sh writes from .env and Compose mounts as <NAME>_FILE, rather than as environment variables; after changing one in .env, re-run ./setup.sh so they match. Re-running also rewrites kendo-app.env from its example (the previous copy is kept as kendo-app.env.bak), keeping every setting you already set: only the domain answer and any key a release added to the example are new. One domain answer reaches all three passkey-bound settings (WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, CORS_ORIGINS) and the Traefik Host() rule — an RP_ID typo is the whole "passkeys silently don't work" failure class, so it is worth not typing four times.

TLS is one question with four answers: Let's Encrypt production, Let's Encrypt staging (rehearse a new domain without burning the production rate limit), bring your own certificate, or skip. Orthogonally, the ACME challenge is HTTP-01 (default, needs inbound 80), TLS-ALPN-01 (needs inbound 443 only — the answer when an ISP blocks 80) or DNS-01 (no inbound ports; it prompts for your lego provider slug and prints the credentials that provider wants).

Re-running is safe: existing secrets are carried forward rather than regenerated, and any file it rewrites is kept as .bak. The written files are gitignored, so upgrading cannot revert your domain or email to the shipped placeholders. Prefer doing it by hand? Every file it writes has a documented .example next to it.

The script also checks the five host prerequisites — Podman, the net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=80 sysctl rootless Podman needs to bind 80/443, the firewall, the kendo user and loginctl enable-linger — and prints the exact sudo command for each one that is missing. It never escalates itself; you run those.

3. Check, then start the stack:

./setup.sh check       # green? then:
podman-compose up -d   # pulls ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:0.1

app, proxy and db are restart: always, so a crash or an OOM kill brings them straight back. A reboot does not: rootless Podman has no daemon, and only podman-restart.service (with linger on) starts them again at boot. setup.sh enables it for you (systemctl --user enable podman-restart.service, no sudo), and check fails while it is disabled. It starts every restart: always container, stopped or not, so podman-compose stop does not survive a reboot: use podman-compose down to keep the stack stopped.

check looks at what the app cannot see from inside its container, the things that otherwise surface as a browser error or a certificate that never arrives: placeholder domains, emails or secrets left in .env, kendo-app.env or the Traefik files, a Traefik Host() rule that no longer matches WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, TLS skipped or a bring-your-own certificate not in place, on an SELinux host a bind mount in docker-compose.yml with no z relabel, the domain not resolving to this host, something else already on 80/443, and the five host prerequisites. Each FAIL names its fix; it changes nothing and exits non-zero on any FAIL. A warn is something it cannot decide from here — DNS pointing at a router's public address is right behind NAT — and does not fail it. Run it any time: after an upgrade, after a domain change, or paste its output into a bug report.

KENDO_IMAGE in .env is the pin. The documented default is the Release line tag :0.1: fixes and features, but no Breaking change — nothing that needs a manual step or a restore from backup to undo. Moving to :0.2 is a deliberate edit, made after reading its section in Upgrading. From 1.0 the pin is the major, :1 (ADR-0009).

Contributors still build from source — make build produces localhost/kendodojo:latest; set KENDO_IMAGE=localhost/kendodojo:latest to run it.

Traefik serves the app on 443 and redirects 80 to it. The app service publishes no host port of its own: every request arrives through the proxy, which is what makes TRUST_PROXY_XFF (on by default here) safe — Traefik overwrites X-Forwarded-For with the address it observed, so rate limiting and account lockout see a client IP the client cannot choose. If you re-publish the app's port, set TRUST_PROXY_XFF=false in the same edit.

Alembic migrations run in the migrate service, which runs alembic upgrade head and exits; app starts only once it has succeeded. Uploaded logos and backgrounds persist in the static_uploads named volume, and the database in postgres_data — both survive down/up and image rebuilds.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
An upgrade is three steps: back up, pull the image you pin, restart onto it. Nothing in it touches a deployment file. Once installed, the compose file, the units, the timers, the scripts, the env files and the Traefik config are yours, edits included, and no upgrade step overwrites one (#604).

A release that changes one of those files says so in its release notes, under Operator action. Read the notes before you upgrade, and apply each action first, as Operator actions describes.

docs.title: Quick self-host (Compose)
docs.text:
./setup.sh upgrade

An upgrade runs alembic upgrade head against your live database, so this takes a backup first: deploy/bin/kendo-backup.sh writes the database dump and the uploads tarball to ~/backups and says where. Then it pulls the image KENDO_IMAGE in .env names and recreates the stack on it. It changes none of your files.

After it, podman-compose logs migrate names the schema revision the database started at and the one it is at now, with each revision applied in between (#606).

If the upgrade or the migration fails, it prints the exact kendo-restore.sh command for the backup it just took. It also prints the digest of the image that was running, to pin back to. Restoring the data alone is only half a rollback, because the new image would migrate it straight back up. Run every printed step: the last one re-runs migrate, which the app needs after a restore (#481).

If your backups are encrypted, have the backup key to hand before you start: a rollback restores the backup just taken, and kendo-restore.sh asks for the key. setup.sh upgrade reminds you. See Backups.

Some migrations check your data before changing the schema, and stop if they find rows only you can decide about — for example an account that belongs to no member, or a member whose email differs from the account that signs in as them (#432). They stop before changing anything, name the rows, and say what to fix. Fix those rows, then run ./setup.sh upgrade again.

A plain podman-compose pull && podman-compose up -d is not enough on Podman: podman-compose recreates a container only when the compose file changes, so a new image under the same :0.1 tag never starts.

docs.title: Hardened deployment (Quadlet)
docs.text:
./setup.sh upgrade is the Compose path only. On a Quadlet host, run these steps as kendo:

# Back up first: kendo-migrate runs `alembic upgrade head` against your live
# database. This is the backup to restore if the upgrade fails — see
# Backups § Restore.
systemctl --user start kendo-backup.service

# Pull every image the three Release units pin. Restarting a unit never
# fetches a newer image under the same tag, so without this nothing changes.
u=~/.config/containers/systemd
sed -n 's/^Image=//p' "$u"/kendo-app.container "$u"/kendo-migrate.container \
  "$u"/kendo-ip-retention.container | sort -u | xargs -n1 podman pull

# Restart onto it: kendo-migrate migrates, then the app starts.
systemctl --user restart kendo-migrate kendo-app

# Make sure Traefik is running. It needs kendo-app (Requires=), so systemd
# stops it whenever the app stops or fails to start, and restarting the app
# does not start it again. When Traefik is already running, this does nothing.
systemctl --user start kendo-traefik

Without that last line, a restart that failed once (say kendo-migrate stopped on an error you then fixed) leaves the app running but the site unreachable: the browser reports it cannot connect (#628).

Then, from your admin account, read what kendo-migrate did: the revision the schema started at, each one applied, and the one it is at now (#606). On a failure it says why. kendo cannot read the journal itself (Deployment § Logs):

sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-migrate.service --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager

If it failed, restore the backup taken above — Backups § Restore.

Traefik and PostgreSQL run images their own units pin. A release that moves one of those pins says so as an Operator action. Once you have edited the unit, pull the new image and add kendo-traefik or kendo-db to the restart.

docs.title: Operator actions
docs.text:
Each release's notes list every change to a deployment file under Operator action, with a Compose heading and a Quadlet heading as each applies. Each says what to change, and what happens if you do not. A new setting that has a safe default needs no action. Apply them before the routine upgrade above, so that its restart picks them up.

To see the release's version of a file, extract the release's bundle into a directory of its own. Never extract it over your install: the bundle's files would replace yours. Set IMAGE to the image you are upgrading to — what Image= in kendo-app.container names on Quadlet, or KENDO_IMAGE in .env on Compose:

podman pull "$IMAGE"
mkdir -p ~/kendo-release
podman run --rm "$IMAGE" init | tar -x -C ~/kendo-release

Compare the file the action names with your copy, and carry the change into yours, keeping your own edits — the firewalld ports of Deployment § 1.2 in kendo-traefik.container, say:

Bundle file Your copy on Compose Your copy on Quadlet Then deploy/quadlet/* — ~/.config/containers/systemd/ systemctl --user daemon-reload, then restart the unit deploy/systemd/* — ~/.config/systemd/user/ systemctl --user daemon-reload; enable --now a new timer deploy/bin/* deploy/bin/ ~/.local/bin/ (install -m 755) nothing: the next backup runs it docker-compose.yml docker-compose.yml — the routine upgrade recreates the stack setup.sh setup.sh ~/src/setup.sh nothing: take it whole, it holds no setting of yours .env.example .env — the routine upgrade deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example kendo-app.env ~/kendo/kendo-app.env the routine upgrade deploy/traefik/selfhost/ deploy/traefik/selfhost/ — Traefik reloads dynamic/ by itself; restart the proxy for traefik.yml deploy/traefik/ — ~/kendo/traefik/ Traefik reloads dynamic/ by itself; restart kendo-traefik for traefik.yml

A changed unit needs the daemon-reload before its restart: Quadlet generates the service from the file only then. An env file needs only the restart.

docs.title: A new setting in the env file
docs.text:
When a release adds a setting without a safe default, its Operator action names it. The app does not see a key that is absent from your env file: the unit and the compose file pass that one file and nothing else. To find every key the release's example has that yours lacks, compare keys, not lines. Values legitimately differ per host, so a plain diff is all noise. On Quadlet:

diff <(grep -oE '^[A-Z0-9_]+=' ~/kendo/kendo-app.env | tr -d = | sort) \
     <(grep -oE '^[A-Z0-9_]+=' ~/kendo-release/deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example | tr -d = | sort)

On Compose, compare kendo-app.env in the install directory instead. Empty output means nothing new. A > line is a setting you lack: copy it across with its comment. Then, once the routine upgrade has restarted the app, check that the app received it. A restart proves the unit started, not that the value arrived:

podman exec kendo-app printenv APP_ENV JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES   # Quadlet
podman-compose exec app printenv APP_ENV JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES # Compose
# APP_ENV=production
# JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES=480

docs.title: Pinning a Version, and rolling back
docs.text:
The units pin the Release line's moving tag, :0.1, so the routine upgrade takes each patch release. To run an exact Version instead, such as a release candidate or the one you ran before, edit the pin. Then run the routine upgrade, which pulls what the pin names.

On Quadlet, the pin is Image= in kendo-app.container, kendo-migrate.container and kendo-ip-retention.container. Keep the three the same:

TAG=0.1.0-rc3   # the tag to run
cd ~/.config/containers/systemd
sed -i "s|^Image=.*|Image=ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:$TAG|" \
  kendo-app.container kendo-migrate.container kendo-ip-retention.container
systemctl --user daemon-reload

On Compose, the pin is KENDO_IMAGE in .env: the image name, a colon and the tag.

Rolling back is the same edit, back to the tag you ran before. A migration has to be undone too, so restore the backup the upgrade took, after the edit: Backups § Restore ends by restarting kendo-migrate, on the image the pin now names. A failed ./setup.sh upgrade prints these steps for you, with the digest of the image that was running.

docs.title: Checking an image came from this repository
docs.text:
Each release image is signed by the release workflow with cosign keyless signing (#457). To check the image you are about to run, with cosign installed:

cosign verify ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:0.1 \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/booji/KendoDojoManagement/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v'

It fails unless the image's digest was signed by that workflow on a release tag. Podman does not check this by itself yet (#518). The signature is recorded in Sigstore's public transparency log, which names this repository, the workflow and the release tag.

docs.title: Upgrading to a new Release line
docs.text:
Within a Release line (:0.1) every upgrade is the routine one above, plus any Operator actions its notes list. The exception is a security fix that cannot avoid breaking: its release notes say so under a Security heading, and the upgrade stops until you have acted. Moving to the next (:0.2) is a Breaking change: it needs a step only you can take, or carries a migration that returning to the previous image cannot undo. Each one gets its own section here, headed "Upgrading to 0.Y", with the operator action its release notes list. Read it before you change the pin.

None yet: 0.1 is the first Release line.

docs.title: From a release candidate: splitting .env once
docs.text:
Quick self-host only, and only for a host set up with v0.1.0-rc1 or v0.1.0-rc2. Those kept every app setting in .env. From v0.1.0-rc3 the app reads its settings from kendo-app.env next to docker-compose.yml instead, written from deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example, the file the hardened deployment uses too (#603). .env keeps only the image pin, the db settings and the secrets. ./setup.sh upgrade stops, before it backs up or changes anything, while kendo-app.env is missing.

.env pins the rc it was set up with, so first point KENDO_IMAGE at the release (Pinning a Version). Extract that release's bundle, as Operator actions describes. Then, in the directory that holds .env, take its setup.sh, compose file and env example, and create kendo-app.env once:

cp ~/kendo-release/setup.sh setup.sh
cp ~/kendo-release/docker-compose.yml docker-compose.yml
mkdir -p deploy/env
cp ~/kendo-release/deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example deploy/env/
cp deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example kendo-app.env

The rc's own setup.sh upgrade would refresh the bundle itself and recreate the stack without kendo-app.env; the new one does neither.

If you had edited docker-compose.yml (a BYO certificate's mount, say), make the same edit again in the new one.

Then copy your own values from .env into kendo-app.env, key for key: WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, CORS_ORIGINS and TZ always, and any other app setting you changed from its default (JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES, SESSION_MAX_MINUTES, the *_MIN_DURATION_MS floors and so on). A wrong WEBAUTHN_* value here makes every passkey ceremony fail, so check those three against your domain. Leave the secrets in .env: DATABASE_URL, MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, SETUP_TOKEN and POSTGRES_* never go in kendo-app.env, because the app reads that file whole and must never see the superuser login (ADR-0007).

The app settings left in .env are ignored from now on. Delete them, so that nobody tunes a value there that never reaches the app. Keep KENDO_IMAGE, TZ (the db's), POSTGRES_*, MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL, DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET and SETUP_TOKEN. Then upgrade as usual:

./setup.sh upgrade
./setup.sh check

docs.title: From v0.1.0-rc1 on Quadlet: installing the backup units once
docs.text:
A Quadlet host set up with v0.1.0-rc1 has no backup units: setup.sh --quadlet installs them from v0.1.0-rc2 (#576). Without them the routine upgrade's first step fails. Install them once, as kendo, from the release's bundle extracted as Operator actions describes:

cd ~/kendo-release
install -m 755 deploy/bin/kendo-backup.sh deploy/bin/kendo-restore.sh ~/.local/bin/
cp deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.service deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.timer ~/.config/systemd/user/
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now kendo-backup.timer

docs.title: Break-glass recovery
docs.text:
Use this when the only admin is locked out and has no recovery codes.

podman exec kendo-app python -m app.cli create-recovery-token <email>

This prints a single-use plaintext token valid for 60 minutes. Redeem it at:

  • API: POST /auth/recovery/redeem — body {"email": "<email>", "code": "<token>"}
  • Login page: enter the email and paste the token into the recovery code field

The command refuses a Member whose Membership Status is archived or suspended, because they cannot sign in. Reinstate them first by setting membership_status to active.

Security notes: - Run this command on the server only — never over an untrusted network. - The token is stored as a bcrypt hash; the plaintext is never persisted. - Delete the token from your terminal history after use.

docs.title: Claim the admin account (the setup token gates it)
docs.text:
On the quick self-host the token is SETUP_TOKEN in .env, and the commands below that name kendo-app or a podman secret are the Quadlet spellings: the claim itself is the same request either way.

The instance is now reachable. Claiming the first admin account requires the kendo_setup_token secret from section 2-4 — the setup endpoints answer 401 {"detail": "Invalid setup token"} without it (ADR-0003). Nothing to race: an opportunistic scanner that finds the host minutes after Traefik's Let's Encrypt certificate hits the certificate transparency logs cannot claim anything without that value.

The token is required whether or not the instance is already claimed: the app refuses to start without it, so do not delete the secret after claiming. A database restore or wipe would otherwise boot an unclaimed instance with no gate in front of it.

The browser is the way you do this. Open https://<your-domain>/: the setup page asks for the admin's first name, surname and email, and the setup token. The claim creates the admin's member record as well as their account — every account belongs to a member, the first admin included — and the email is the one they will sign in with. Paste the token into the "Setup token" field and complete the passkey registration. The page sends it as an X-Setup-Token header on /api/setup/passkey/begin and /api/setup/passkey/complete, and a wrong token comes back on the form as "Invalid setup token". The value is never stored in the browser — reloading the page means pasting it again.

No shell access is needed to claim the account, so the URL and the token can go to whoever is becoming the admin. The curl below is for debugging a claim that is not working, not a step:

curl -sS -X POST https://<your-domain>/api/setup/passkey/begin \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-Setup-Token: $SETUP_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"email":"admin@your-dojo","first_name":"Ai","surname":"Sato"}'
# 401 {"detail":"Invalid setup token"} -> wrong or missing token.
# 404 {"detail":"Setup already completed"} -> claimed; the token is irrelevant.

Then confirm the window is shut.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<your-domain>/api/setup
# 404 -> setup is closed, an account exists.
# 200 -> still unclaimed (the token is still required to claim it).
# anything else (000, 502, ...) -> the check never reached the app. That is not
# a closed window; fix the request and re-run before you believe it.

The instance is claimed once an Admin Account exists, and stays claimed even if that Admin later deletes every passkey. An abandoned ceremony leaves only a member Account, which does not count, so an operator whose browser died mid-ceremony is never locked out.

Lost the token? Rotate it — nothing in the database has to change:

# Keep the value: a podman secret cannot be read back, so piping straight into
# `secret create` leaves you with a token nobody knows.
token=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n')
podman secret rm kendo_setup_token
printf '%s' "$token" | podman secret create kendo_setup_token -
systemctl --user restart kendo-app
echo "$token"   # hand it over out of band, then clear your scrollback

app/cli.py create-recovery-token does not cover a never-claimed instance: it resolves an Account by email, and an unclaimed instance has none. Rotation is the only path there, and it costs seconds.

docs.title: Day-2 operations
docs.text:
Task Command (as kendo via machinectl shell kendo@ /bin/bash) Status systemctl --user status kendo-app --no-pager Logs podman logs -f kendo-app A unit's journal (why it failed) From your admin account, not kendo, which cannot read the journal: sudo journalctl _UID=$(id -u kendo) _SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT=kendo-app.service --no-pager; swap in any unit. See Deployment § Logs Restart app systemctl --user restart kendo-app Upgrade Follow Upgrading § Hardened deployment: back up, pull the pinned image, restart — a restart without the pull is not a patch. Apply the release notes' Operator actions first Stop all systemctl --user stop kendo-ip-retention.timer kendo-backup.timer kendo-traefik kendo-app kendo-migrate kendo-db — the timers first, or their next run starts kendo-db again Back up now systemctl --user start kendo-backup.service New backup key — see Backups ./setup.sh backup-key --quadlet (from the deployment bundle) Break-glass recovery podman exec kendo-app python -m app.cli create-recovery-token <email>

The pin is the Image= line in the three app-image Quadlet units (kendo-app, kendo-migrate, kendo-ip-retention), and the documented value is the Release line tag :0.1 — fixes and features, but no Breaking change. Moving to :0.2 is a deliberate edit made after reading its section in Upgrading. Building from source still works (podman build -t localhost/kendodojo:latest .); point Image= at it.

docs.title: Container architecture
docs.text:
File Purpose Dockerfile Multi-stage build: backend-deps → backend-dev-deps → frontend-deps → frontend-build → prod docker-compose.yml Production stack (app + PostgreSQL, named volumes for db data and uploads) docker-compose.dev.yml Dev stack with bind-mounted source and hot-reload docker-compose.test.yml Test watcher stack with ephemeral PostgreSQL .env.example Template for the production stack's .env: image pin, db settings and secrets deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example Template for the app settings (kendo-app.env), shared with the Quadlet deployment .env.dev Dev defaults (safe to commit) .env.test Test defaults (safe to commit)

Each stack sets an explicit Compose project name — kendodojo, kendodojo-dev and kendodojo-test. Without it Compose derives the name from the directory, so all three resolved to the same containers, networks and volumes: starting the dev database silently replaced the test one, and down on either file removed containers belonging to the other.

If you have a checkout from before this change, your old containers and volumes are still named after the directory (kendodojomanagement_*) and are now orphaned. To carry dev data across:

podman exec kendodojomanagement_db_1 pg_dump -U kendo_dev -d kendo_dev > dev.sql
podman rm -f kendodojomanagement_db_1
podman-compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file .env.dev up -d db
podman exec -i kendodojo-dev_db_1 psql -U kendo_dev -d kendo_dev < dev.sql
podman volume rm kendodojomanagement_postgres_dev_data   # once you are happy

Nothing needs carrying across for the test stack — its database is deliberately volume-less and is rebuilt on every run.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
The two env templates are the reference: every variable is documented in place, next to the value it ships with. They are included here as they are in the release you are reading.

Both deployments take their app settings from the same template, deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example. They differ only in where the secrets come from.

docs.title: App settings — kendo-app.env
docs.text:
Non-sensitive settings only. The quick self-host keeps the file next to docker-compose.yml, and the hardened deployment at ~/kendo/kendo-app.env. ./setup.sh writes it from this template on both paths, filling in the domain. The container reads the whole file, so every key in it reaches the app.

DATABASE_URL, MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET and SETUP_TOKEN are not in this file: see below for the quick self-host, and Hardened deployment for the podman secrets.

# Non-sensitive app config for UAT/PROD. Copy to ~kendo/kendo/kendo-app.env and
# edit the domain values. Secrets (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET) are NOT here — they
# are podman secrets the Quadlet unit mounts as files (<NAME>_FILE, #462).
#
# Per-host file: UAT and PROD differ ONLY in the domain-derived values below.

# Selects the production config path in app/config.py: with this unset the app
# falls back to "development" and skips every WebAuthn RP ID / origin shape
# check in validate_startup_config(), so a placeholder domain or an http://
# origin boots cleanly and only fails in the browser (#385). The Quadlet unit
# passes this file and nothing else, so it has to be set here.
APP_ENV=production

# Container timezone (IANA name). Sets local time for the app; keep the db
# (deploy/quadlet/kendo-db.container) in sync. Defaults to UTC if unset.
TZ=Europe/London

# Public domain (no scheme, no port) — must match the Traefik Host() rule.
WEBAUTHN_RP_ID=dojo.example.com
WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN=https://dojo.example.com

# Same-origin SPA, so CORS is effectively inert — but keep it pinned to the one
# canonical origin (never "*"). Fails closed if a cross-origin path ever appears.
CORS_ORIGINS=https://dojo.example.com

# TLS terminates at Traefik; cookies must still be Secure.
COOKIE_SECURE=true

# Trust X-Forwarded-For for client IP (rate limiting). MUST be true
# here because the app sits behind Traefik; leaving it false collapses per-client
# limits into one global bucket. Safe: the app publishes no ports and is only
# reachable via Traefik, which overwrites the header.
TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true

# The idle timeout: an Auth Session unused for this long ends (ADR-0008). One in
# use slides forward, so this is a gap of inactivity rather than a cut-off
# mid-work. The slide is written only past half the window, so the idle window
# a user sees is between half this value and all of it (4-8 hours at 480). The
# name predates server-side sessions and is kept. 480 matches app/config.py.
JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES=480
# The ceiling on one session however continuously it is used: past it the
# Auth Session ends and the user signs in again (one passkey touch). Without it,
# sliding means "signed in forever". 10080 = 7 days.
SESSION_MAX_MINUTES=10080
WEBAUTHN_CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS=300
# Minimum wall-clock time (ms) the passkey begin endpoints take, regardless of
# whether the email is known/registered or not. Prevents timing-based email
# enumeration; it only masks anything while the real path (commit+fsync
# included) finishes underneath it. 100ms is measured against PostgreSQL, not
# guessed: real-path p99 16.8ms, worst observed 27.9ms, the rest headroom for
# slower storage than the box it was measured on. Alert on the app log's
# "Constant-time floor exceeded" warning — that is the signal this floor has
# stopped protecting anything. See docs/auth-timing-calibration.md.
AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS=100
# Floors for passkey login completion and recovery-code redemption, measured
# the same way (#594). A successful login's worst request took 105ms; a
# redeem runs nine bcrypt comparisons, p99 2.3s, 3.0s at 4 in flight.
LOGIN_COMPLETE_MIN_DURATION_MS=250
